entry.title: Hands-On OpenSearch Storage Tiering: A Log Analytics Implementation
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2026/11/12

This blog post is a hands-on implementation of storage tiering in OpenSearch, using a log analytics scenario based on my experience. In the example, log indexes move through three tiers: hot nodes on local NVMe for the first 3 days, warm nodes on EBS until 90 days, and S3 snapshots that come back as searchable snapshots only when someone needs old data. You will configure the node attributes, index template, and Index State Management (ISM) policy that automate the flow, and see how I run the searchable tier on short-lived Kubernetes nodes and which costs and failures I ran into.

Why I Split the Cluster Into Tiers

I built the tiering for two reasons: cost and performance. Logs have an inconvenient access pattern. The newest data is queried all the time, the oldest is almost never touched, and you still have to keep it. My hot tier runs on EC2 Instance Store (local NVMe), the approach I described in OpenSearch + EC2 Instance Store: A Disruptive Approach to Hot Tier Storage. Local NVMe gave the best performance for data up to 3 days old. After that, queries become rare enough that cheaper EBS disks on warm nodes handle them well.

Long-term retention was harder, because for years OpenSearch had no good answer for it. I wanted searchable snapshots before the feature existed, and in the meantime I kept an in-house solution of Python and shell scripts that duplicated every log into OpenSearch and into S3 as a raw long-term copy. It was horrible to maintain. Even then, I took snapshots of every index, betting on the Searchable Remote Index RFC that was open in the project.

Searchable snapshots shipped as experimental in OpenSearch 2.4 and became generally available in 2.7, in May 2023. I was possibly one of the first to run them in production, and that is where I learned how they work in practice. Some of what I learned was missing from the documentation, so I contributed it: PR #4597 documented the search node role on the cluster setup page and fixed the searchable snapshot example, and PR #12892 documented that node.search.cache.size accepts a percentage.

Tiers Are Node Attributes You Define

Apart from the warm node role used by searchable snapshots, OpenSearch does not know what a hot or warm tier is. Hot, warm, and cold are a naming convention for a setup with three storage layers. Whoever runs the cluster decides how many layers it has, what hardware each one uses, and what to call them. Two layers is a valid design, and so is five.

Tiering in OpenSearch rests on node attributes. Each data node carries a custom attribute that you choose, such as node.attr.temp: hot, and each index carries an allocation filter that requires a value of that attribute. OpenSearch places the index’s shards only on nodes whose attribute matches the filter. To move an index to another tier, you change the filter, and OpenSearch relocates the shards to the nodes that match. The index template and the ISM policy in the rest of this post exist to set that filter and change it at the right time.

Three Tiers for Log Analytics

Tier

Hardware profile

Role

Typical retention for log analytics

Hot

Local NVMe (Instance Store), high CPU, limited capacity

Active indexing and near-real-time search

First 3 days

Warm

Large network-attached disk (EBS), lower CPU

Long-term retention, slower queries

Up to 90 days

Searchable (cold)

On-demand nodes backed by object storage (S3)

Rarely queried data, restored on demand

As long as the snapshot is kept

The table describes a common OpenSearch scenario, log analytics, which is the one I have experience with. The retention values are an example from that scenario, not a rule. In any setup the hot tier should hold a much shorter window than the other tiers, and the exact values depend on how your data is queried.

Data flows in one direction. Fresh logs land on hot nodes, roll over and move to warm nodes after a few days, get snapshotted to S3, and are eventually deleted from the cluster. The snapshot stays in S3, and when someone needs that data again it comes back as a searchable snapshot, pulled into compute only while it is being queried.

Prerequisites: Label Your Nodes

From here on, the post builds the log analytics example step by step, with indexes named my-logs-*. Tag each data node with a custom attribute, conventionally temp, so OpenSearch knows which nodes are hot and which are warm. Set it in each node’s opensearch.yml, or through the environment if you run in containers:

# On every hot data node
node.attr.temp: hot

# On every warm data node
node.attr.temp: warm

The attribute name is arbitrary. What matters is that it is consistent across the cluster, because OpenSearch uses it later to pin shards to a tier. Shard allocation awareness in Step 1 needs a second attribute with the node’s availability zone, for example node.attr.zone: us-east-1a.

For the searchable tier, you need at least one node with the warm node role. That role is what hosts searchable snapshots. A warm node reserves part of its disk as a cache for the snapshot data it reads from S3, sized by node.search.cache.size. The value is a byte size such as 50gb or a percentage of the disk such as 10%. On a node that has only the warm role, it defaults to 80% of the available storage, according to the searchable snapshots documentation:

# On every searchable snapshot node
node.roles: [ warm ]
# Optional on a dedicated node, where the default is 80% of the disk
node.search.cache.size: 80%

About the naming overlap:

The warm node role is the OpenSearch feature behind searchable snapshots. In OpenSearch 2.x it was called search, and the rename was a breaking change in 3.0: the search role now means something else (nodes for search-only shards), so update node roles before upgrading. None of this is related to the custom node.attr.temp: warm attribute used for the EBS warm tier. In most deployments these are separate node groups.

Step 1: Set Up Shard Allocation Awareness

Before moving data around, make sure a shard’s copies are spread across availability zones. This is independent of tiering, but you do not want a primary and its replica in the same zone. Once every node has node.attr.zone set, tell OpenSearch to use it:

PUT _cluster/settings
{
  "persistent": {
    "cluster.routing.allocation.awareness.attributes": "zone"
  }
}

With this in place, OpenSearch places the copies of each shard in different zones, so losing one zone does not lose data, as long as the index has at least one replica.

Step 2: Pin New Indexes to the Hot Tier

Every new index should land on hot nodes. A shard allocation filter is an index setting that restricts which nodes can hold the index’s shards, based on node attributes. You don’t set it per index by hand. You put it in an index template, so every index matching the pattern inherits it:

PUT _index_template/my-logs-template
{
  "index_patterns": ["my-logs-*"],
  "template": {
    "settings": {
      "index.routing.allocation.require.temp": "hot",
      "plugins.index_state_management.rollover_alias": "my-logs"
    }
  }
}

The require filter means shards can only be placed on nodes whose temp attribute equals hot. It is one of several allocation deciders that OpenSearch checks before placing a shard, alongside disk watermarks, which I covered in OpenSearch Shard Allocation: Balanced by Count, Rebalanced by Watermarks. That post also explains why global watermarks are a problem in a tiered cluster like this one. The rollover_alias setting tells ISM which alias to roll over, which Step 6 uses.

Step 3: Understand the ISM State Machine

Index State Management (ISM) is the OpenSearch plugin that automates operations on indexes as they age, and it is the engine behind automatic tiering. An ISM policy is a small state machine with three building blocks:

  • State: a status the index can be in, such as hot, warm, or delete. An index is in exactly one state at a time.

  • Action: an operation that runs when the index enters a state, such as rollover, snapshot, replica_count, allocation, or delete. Actions run in the order you declare them.

  • Transition: the condition that moves the index to the next state, for example reaching a minimum age.

Once a policy is attached, ISM runs a background job for each managed index, every 5 minutes by default (ISM settings). The job runs the current state’s actions, evaluates the transition conditions, and moves the index forward when they are met.

Step 4: Register the S3 Snapshot Repository

Before an index is deleted from the cluster, the policy copies it to S3 with a snapshot, so the repository has to exist before the policy runs. Register it once:

PUT _snapshot/logs-s3-repository
{
  "type": "s3",
  "settings": {
    "bucket": "my-opensearch-snapshots",
    "base_path": "logs"
  }
}

Step 5: Write the Tiering Policy

Here is the complete hot to warm to delete policy, with the snapshot to S3 in the warm state:

PUT _plugins/_ism/policies/logs_tiering_policy
{
  "policy": {
    "description": "Hot -> Warm -> Delete lifecycle for time-series logs",
    "default_state": "hot",
    "states": [
      {
        "name": "hot",
        "actions": [
          {
            "rollover": {
              "min_index_age": "3d",
              "min_primary_shard_size": "50gb"
            }
          }
        ],
        "transitions": [
          {
            "state_name": "warm"
          }
        ]
      },
      {
        "name": "warm",
        "actions": [
          {
            "replica_count": {
              "number_of_replicas": 1
            }
          },
          {
            "allocation": {
              "require": { "temp": "warm" }
            }
          },
          {
            "snapshot": {
              "repository": "logs-s3-repository",
              "snapshot": "{{ctx.index}}"
            }
          }
        ],
        "transitions": [
          {
            "state_name": "delete",
            "conditions": {
              "min_index_age": "90d"
            }
          }
        ]
      },
      {
        "name": "delete",
        "actions": [
          {
            "delete": {}
          }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "ism_template": {
      "index_patterns": ["my-logs-*"],
      "priority": 100
    }
  }
}

In the hot state, the rollover action creates a new write index once the current one is 3 days old or its primary shard reaches 50 GB, whichever comes first. The hot transition has no condition, so right after the rollover the old index moves to warm.

In the warm state, three actions run in order. replica_count sets the replicas to 1, because older data needs less redundancy headroom and the saved disk adds up. Then allocation with require: { temp: warm } replaces the hot filter from the template, and OpenSearch relocates the shards to the warm (EBS) nodes. Last, snapshot copies the index to the logs-s3-repository repository. The index stays on the warm nodes until it is 90 days old, then the delete state removes it from the cluster. The snapshot in S3 is not touched, and Step 7 brings it back when needed.

The ism_template block attaches the policy to every new index that matches my-logs-*, so you never attach it by hand. It only applies to indexes created after the policy exists, which is why the policy comes before the first index.

Step 6: Bootstrap the First Index and the Write Alias

The rollover action needs a write alias that it can move from the current index to the next one. Create the first index with that alias:

PUT my-logs-000001
{
  "aliases": {
    "my-logs": {
      "is_write_index": true
    }
  }
}

The index inherits the hot allocation filter and the rollover alias from the template, and the ISM policy from the ism_template. From now on, your application writes to the my-logs alias, never to a specific index. When the rollover fires, OpenSearch creates my-logs-000002, moves the write alias to it, and ISM starts moving the old index to warm.

Confirm that the shards landed on hot nodes and that the policy is attached:

GET _cat/shards/my-logs-000001?v
GET _plugins/_ism/explain/my-logs-000001

Step 7: Restore Old Data as a Searchable Snapshot

The policy deletes each index from the cluster at 90 days, but its snapshot stays in S3. Often you must keep old data longer, for compliance or for the occasional investigation, without paying for warm nodes to hold it. A searchable snapshot is an index restored from a snapshot repository while its data stays in remote storage, such as S3. Compute is attached only when someone queries it.

ISM appends a timestamp to the snapshot name, so the snapshot for my-logs-000001 is named something like my-logs-000001-2026.11.15-14:05:12.345. List the repository to find the exact name before restoring:

GET _cat/snapshots/logs-s3-repository?v

After the index is deleted from the cluster, you can bring it back on demand as a searchable snapshot:

POST _snapshot/logs-s3-repository/<snapshot-name>/_restore
{
  "storage_type": "remote_snapshot",
  "indices": "my-logs-000001",
  "index_settings": {
    "index.number_of_replicas": 0
  }
}

storage_type: remote_snapshot is the difference from a normal restore. Instead of downloading the whole index to local disk, OpenSearch loads the index into the cluster while S3 remains the authoritative copy of the data, and it downloads and caches segments locally as queries need them. This requires at least one node with the warm role from the prerequisites.

I restore searchable snapshots with zero replicas. The snapshot was taken in the warm state with 1 replica, and without index_settings the restored index keeps that value. A replica would only duplicate a cache, because the data is already safe in S3. The trade-off is availability: if the node holding the shard goes down, the index is unavailable and the cluster turns red until the node comes back. When it rejoins, OpenSearch allocates the shard again from the snapshot in S3. For an index that someone queries during an occasional investigation, I accept that.

How I Run the Searchable Tier on Kubernetes

I don’t keep warm-role nodes running all the time. When a process needed logs that had already been rotated to S3, I created a Karpenter NodePool only for searchable snapshots, brought up an OpenSearch node with the warm role on it, restored the snapshots, and removed the NodePool once the work was done. I paid for that compute only while someone was looking at old data.

That node used Instance Store, not EBS. The local disk on a warm node only holds the cache of data read from S3, and S3 is what guarantees durability. Paying for EBS durability on a disk that only holds a cache made no sense to me. If the node disappears, the cache goes with it, and the data is still in S3.

Test Searchable Snapshots on Every Upgrade

The worst problem I had with this setup came from an OpenSearch upgrade. After one version bump, the restore behavior of searchable snapshots changed and restores started failing with errors. It turned out to be a bug in that version, and a later release fixed it.

Searchable snapshots are the tier you touch least, which makes them easy to forget in an upgrade checklist. If they matter to you, add a test to every OpenSearch upgrade: restore a known snapshot with storage_type: remote_snapshot and run a query against it before you call the upgrade done.

Operational Tips

  • Watch the transitions. GET _plugins/_ism/explain/<index> shows the state of each managed index and why it has not transitioned yet.

  • Monitor shard movement. While indexes move from hot to warm, GET _cat/shards?v&s=state shows RELOCATING shards. Large migrations consume I/O and network, so schedule big retention changes off-peak. The same relocation mechanics apply when you remove nodes, as in Scaling Down and Resizing OpenSearch Data Nodes Without Losing Data.

  • Size rollover by shard size, not only by age. A 50 GB primary shard cap keeps shards in a healthy range through traffic spikes. Keep the age condition too, so quiet indexes still roll over.

  • Keep at least one replica on hot. The hot tier is where you can least afford data loss, especially on ephemeral local NVMe. If replicas are new to you, start with OpenSearch Concepts: Index and Shards. Drop to zero replicas only on tiers where you can restore from a snapshot.

  • ISM pauses on red. ISM does not run jobs while the cluster health is red. If transitions seem stuck, check cluster health first.

What I Would Do Differently

If I built this again, I would start by trying to simplify as much as possible and asking whether I really need several storage layers. Each tier adds complexity, and each one consumes CPU, memory, and above all network. Every index that moves from hot to warm is copied across the network, replicas are copied again, and snapshots are uploaded to S3. On AWS that traffic shows up on the bill. In my experience, replication and data migration between tiers can increase AWS costs considerably, enough that a three-tier design is worth justifying with your own access patterns before you build it.

When the access pattern does justify it, as it did for me, tiering works well. New data stays fast on NVMe, older data gets cheap on EBS, and the oldest data costs only S3 storage until someone needs it. The searchable tier also replaced the in-house scripts I used to maintain with a restore call.

Key Takeaways

  • Hot, warm, and cold are a convention. The cluster admin defines how many storage layers exist, and each layer is a value of a custom node attribute (node.attr.temp) that shard allocation filters require.

  • An index template pins new indexes to hot nodes and sets the rollover alias. The ISM policy moves them to warm by replacing that filter.

  • Create the ISM policy before the first index, because ism_template only attaches to indexes created after it.

  • The ISM snapshot action copies each index to S3 before deletion, and appends a timestamp to the snapshot name.

  • Restoring with storage_type: remote_snapshot keeps the data in S3 and needs nodes with the warm role (search in OpenSearch 2.x). Their cache size is set with node.search.cache.size.

  • Searchable snapshot nodes can be short-lived and run on Instance Store, because their disk only holds a cache and S3 holds the data.

  • Test a searchable snapshot restore on every OpenSearch upgrade. A version bug once broke my restores after an upgrade.

  • Each tier costs CPU, memory, and network. On AWS, replication and migration between tiers can raise the bill considerably, so justify every layer.

References

  • Index State Management (OpenSearch)

  • ISM policies (OpenSearch)

  • ISM settings (OpenSearch)

  • Index templates (OpenSearch)

  • Take and restore snapshots (OpenSearch)

  • Searchable snapshots (OpenSearch)

  • Breaking changes in 3.0 (OpenSearch)

  • Cluster routing and awareness (OpenSearch)

  • Searchable snapshots are generally available in OpenSearch 2.7 (OpenSearch blog)

  • RFC: Searchable Remote Index (OpenSearch GitHub)

entry.title: Avoiding Over-Sharding in OpenSearch with Filtered Aliases per Environment
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2026/11/11

This blog post covers one of the strategies I use to avoid over-sharding in OpenSearch. Instead of per-environment indexes, I write all logs into one index series and expose each environment as a filtered alias. The rule behind it is simple: the environment is an attribute of each document, so it belongs in a field, not in the index name. The cluster keeps fewer, fuller shards and one mapping, and OpenSearch Dashboards users still get a per-environment view that behaves like a dedicated index.

Too Many Small Shards: The Problem With Per-Environment Indexes

The instinct is to give every environment its own index, and I used to do exactly that:

my-app-logs-dev
my-app-logs-stage
my-app-logs-sandbox
my-app-logs-prod
...

It looks tidy, but it scales badly. Every index has a footprint, even an empty one. Each shard is a Lucene index. It uses heap and file handles and takes up space in the cluster state. A dev environment that gets a trickle of logs still gets the shard count your template sets, so a 50 MB index can end up split into several half-empty shards. Multiply that by every environment and every log type, and the cluster carries hundreds of nearly empty shards for no benefit. That is over-sharding.

Small shards also cause the problem I described in my post about shard allocation and disk watermarks. The default allocator balances shards by count, not by size. In a cluster with many small, granular indexes, one node can hold dozens of tiny shards and use very little disk, while another holds a few large shards and is almost full. The shard distribution looks balanced, but disk usage tells a different story, and the disk watermarks end up doing the balancing work. Per-environment indexes are an easy way to end up there, so they are one of the first things I avoid when I design index templates.

Splitting the data also makes it harder to query. To look at all environments, or a subset of them, someone has to know which indexes exist and target them with wildcards or comma-separated lists.

The data has the same shape in every environment: the same application’s logs, coming from a different cluster. That makes the environment an attribute of each record, so I model it as a field. It looks like a minor decision, but it saves a lot of operational work later.

How Filtered Aliases Split One Index by Environment

A filtered alias is an alias with a query filter attached. According to the OpenSearch documentation, the filter applies to every search, count, and delete-by-query call that goes through the alias. For example, my-app-logs-prod points at the my-app-logs indexes with a filter of environment: prod. A query on my-app-logs-prod returns only production documents, even though all environments share the same indexes.

An alias doesn’t copy data or add shards. The cluster holds one index series and a handful of alias definitions.

Defining the Aliases in an Index Template

An index template is a set of settings, mappings, and aliases that OpenSearch applies to every new index whose name matches its pattern. The aliases belong in the index template, not in a one-off _aliases call. An alias added through the API attaches only to the indexes that exist at that moment, even with a wildcard pattern. Indexes created later are not added. With the aliases in the template, every new index in the series carries them from the start:

PUT _index_template/my-app-logs
{
  "index_patterns": ["my-app-logs*"],
  "template": {
    "settings": {
      "index.number_of_shards": "4",
      "index.number_of_replicas": "1",
      "index.refresh_interval": "10s",
      "index.routing.allocation.require.temp": "hot",
      "plugins.index_state_management.rollover_alias": "my-app-logs"
    },
    "aliases": {
      "my-app-logs-dev": {
        "is_write_index": false,
        "filter": { "term": { "environment": "dev" } }
      },
      "my-app-logs-stage": {
        "is_write_index": false,
        "filter": { "term": { "environment": "stage" } }
      },
      "my-app-logs-sandbox": {
        "is_write_index": false,
        "filter": { "term": { "environment": "sandbox" } }
      },
      "my-app-logs-prod": {
        "is_write_index": false,
        "filter": { "term": { "environment": "prod" } }
      }
    }
  },
  "composed_of": [
    "settings-default",
    "default-mappings",
    "kubernetes-mappings",
    "my-app-logs-mappings"
  ]
}

Each environment alias pairs is_write_index: false with a term filter. The aliases are read-only views, and nothing writes through them. term is an exact-match query, so my-app-logs-prod resolves to the documents whose environment is exactly prod. For that to work, environment must be mapped as a keyword field in one of the component templates. On an analyzed text field, a term filter can silently miss documents.

The shared settings and mappings come from the component templates listed in composed_of. Because every environment writes into the same indexes, they all get the same field mappings. Two environments can no longer drift apart, which is a common problem when each one has its own index.

Writes go through a single rollover alias, my-app-logs. A rollover alias is the alias that ISM moves to a new index each time the current one gets too big or too old. Here it is set in plugins.index_state_management.rollover_alias and managed by an ISM policy. Create the first index with that alias as the write index, as you would for any rollover setup:

PUT my-app-logs-000001
{
  "aliases": {
    "my-app-logs": {
      "is_write_index": true
    }
  }
}

The log shipper in each environment’s cluster writes to my-app-logs and sets the environment field from the cluster it runs in. ISM rolls the series over by size or age (my-app-logs-000001, my-app-logs-000002, …). Because the environment aliases live in the template, each new index starts with all of them attached.

Per-Environment Views in OpenSearch Dashboards

The people reading the logs benefit the most from this pattern. In Dashboards, create one index pattern per environment alias. my-app-logs-prod shows only production logs, and my-app-logs-stage shows only staging. An index pattern of my-app-logs* shows every environment in one place.

To an analyst, my-app-logs-prod looks and behaves like a dedicated production index, with the same fields and search experience, scoped to production. They don’t need to know it is a filtered view. Cross-environment questions such as “show me this error in stage and production” are easy to answer because the data was never split up.

Per-Environment Indexes vs. Filtered Aliases

Concern

Per-environment indexes

Unified index + filtered aliases

Shard and cluster-state footprint

One or more shards per environment, even tiny ones

One index’s shards, shared by all environments

Small environments

Under-filled shards wasting heap and disk

No dedicated footprint, just an alias

Cross-environment queries

Wildcards or comma lists across many indexes

One index series, optionally filtered

Per-environment view

Natural

Preserved through the filtered alias

Mapping consistency

Can drift between environments

One shared mapping

Rollover and ISM

One rollover series per environment

One rollover series

When to Use Separate Indexes Anyway

A filtered alias is a read convenience over shared storage. When environments need real physical separation, use separate indexes:

  • Hard isolation and access control. If production and dev must live on different storage tiers, or a user must never be able to touch production shards, an alias filter is not a security boundary. Anyone allowed to read the underlying indexes can query them directly and skip the filter. If you only need to restrict which documents a role can read, the Security plugin’s document-level security does that on a shared index.

  • Very different retention or sizing. Say production needs 180 days of retention on large shards and dev needs 2 days on small ones. Separate index series with their own ISM policies are cleaner than one policy for everything.

  • Very different volume. If one environment produces far more data than the others and needs a different shard layout, splitting it out can be justified.

The common case is the same log type coming from several environments with similar retention and mappings. For that, I use this pattern almost by default: one index series, one mapping, one rollover alias, and as many per-environment views as you need.

Key Takeaways

  • Model the environment as a field. Every environment’s logs have the same shape, so they belong in the same index series.

  • One index per environment multiplies under-filled shards, and each one costs heap, file handles, and cluster state even when it holds almost no data.

  • Fewer, fuller shards keep count-based shard balancing closer to real disk usage, so the disk watermarks have less to correct.

  • A filtered alias doesn’t copy data. Searches, counts, and delete-by-query through the alias only see documents that match its filter.

  • Define the environment aliases in the index template. Aliases added with the _aliases API do not attach to indexes that rollover creates later.

  • Map environment as a keyword field so the term filter matches exactly.

  • Write through a single rollover alias managed by ISM, and keep the environment aliases read-only with is_write_index: false.

  • An alias filter is not a security boundary. Use document-level security to restrict reads, and separate indexes when an environment needs physical isolation, different retention, or a different shard layout.

References

  • Index aliases (OpenSearch)

  • Index templates (OpenSearch)

  • Term query (OpenSearch)

  • ISM policies (OpenSearch)

  • Document-level security (OpenSearch)

I’m Carlos Neto, and I’ve been running OpenSearch on EKS for over five years. More about me on my home page. If you have questions or a different approach, contact me on LinkedIn.

entry.title: Scaling Down and Resizing OpenSearch Data Nodes Without Losing Data
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2026/11/10

This blog post covers the patterns and API calls I use to scale down and resize OpenSearch data nodes without losing data. The rule behind all of them is simple: the data on a node you remove has to end up somewhere else first. If you take nodes away faster than the cluster can relocate their shards, you lose data.

Why Removing Nodes Is Risky

Scaling down or resizing the data tier is one of the riskiest operations you can perform on an OpenSearch cluster. That is true whether you are shrinking the fleet to cut cost, moving to a different instance type, or replacing nodes that use ephemeral storage. Every time I do it, I treat it that way, and I have never regretted being slow about it.

OpenSearch distributes data as shards across nodes (see OpenSearch Concepts - Index and Shards). When a node disappears abruptly, the cluster has to rebuild the missing shard copies from the ones that survive, which consumes bandwidth, CPU, and I/O. If several nodes go at once, or replica counts are too low, the last copy of a shard can disappear before recovery completes.

Scaling up only adds capacity. Scaling down removes capacity that currently holds data, so every node you take out must have its shards relocated to the survivors before it goes. A resize is a scale-down and a scale-up chained together: you replace a node, or a whole node group, with a different shape, and the same rule applies.

A few concepts come up in every step:

  • Allocation is how OpenSearch decides which node holds each shard. It happens automatically, and you can influence it through the Cluster Settings API.

  • Rebalancing is the background process that moves shards between nodes to keep an even distribution. During a scale-down or resize, you want to pause it to avoid unnecessary shard movement.

  • Draining is using an allocation exclusion to tell OpenSearch to move every shard off a specific node before you remove it. It works for any kind of storage, including Instance Store, because once a node is empty, losing its disk does not matter.

  • Blue/Green is bringing up a parallel set of nodes in the new shape, migrating all data to them, then decommissioning the old set. This is how you resize nodes whose disks do not survive replacement.

The safe path is always the same: control shard allocation explicitly, verify the cluster state before each step, and only then remove nodes.

Use Persistent Settings

All the examples below use persistent cluster settings. Transient settings are cleared after a full cluster restart. If the cluster restarts in the middle of a migration, a transient allocation exclusion silently disappears and OpenSearch starts placing shards on the nodes you were draining. Persistent settings stay until you remove them, which also means you must remember to clear them at the end.

What to Watch During a Migration

Monitoring is essential during shard migrations, especially when increasing recovery concurrency or bandwidth limits. I use the following APIs to track shard relocation progress, identify allocation issues, and watch resource consumption across the cluster:

# All shards, sorted by state 
GET /_cat/shards?v&s=state

# Shards grouped by index 
GET /_cat/shards?v&s=index

# Shards grouped by node 
GET /_cat/shards?v&s=node

# Compact view: index, shard, primary/replica, state, node 
GET /_cat/shards?v&h=index,shard,prirep,state,node&s=index

# Ongoing recoveries with details 
GET /_cat/recovery?active_only=true&detailed=true&bytes=gb&v

# Recovery history, including completed ones 
GET /_cat/recovery?v

# Overall cluster health 
GET /_cluster/health

# Wait for relocations and initializations to finish 
GET /_cluster/health?wait_for_no_relocating_shards=true&wait_for_no_initializing_shards=true

# Pending cluster tasks 
GET /_cat/pending_tasks?v

# Active cluster tasks 
GET /_cat/tasks?v

# Why a shard is unassigned or cannot be allocated 
GET /_cluster/allocation/explain

# Node list and resource information 
GET /_cat/nodes?v&s=name

# Disk usage and shard count per node 
GET /_cat/allocation?v

# Filesystem and JVM statistics 
GET /_nodes/stats/fs,jvm

# Operating system and thread pool statistics 
GET /_nodes/stats/os,thread_pool

# Network transport statistics 
GET /_nodes/stats/transport

The Cluster Allocation Explain API can also investigate a specific shard:

POST /_cluster/allocation/explain
{
  "index": "my-index",
  "shard": 0,
  "primary": true
}

Pay particular attention to filesystem utilization and JVM memory pressure. When increasing recovery concurrency, also monitor network throughput at the infrastructure level, since the OpenSearch transport statistics alone do not give a complete picture of network bandwidth. If nodes start approaching resource limits, reduce recovery concurrency and bandwidth before the migration affects normal cluster operations.

Keep these commands at hand throughout the migration and check them before removing each node. A migration is only complete when the intended nodes are empty, shard recoveries have finished, and the cluster is healthy again.

Speeding Up Shard Relocation

OpenSearch applies conservative limits to shard recovery and relocation so these operations do not consume too many cluster resources. By default, a node allows two concurrent incoming and two concurrent outgoing shard recoveries, and the recovery transfer rate is limited to 40mb per second per node. These limits keep the cluster stable during shard movements, but they can also make large migrations take much longer than necessary.

Shards moved off an excluded node are relocations, so they are throttled by these recovery limits, not by the rebalancing settings. If your cluster has spare CPU, memory, disk I/O, and network capacity, you can raise them:

PUT /_cluster/settings
{
  "persistent": {
    "cluster.routing.allocation.node_concurrent_recoveries": 10,
    "indices.recovery.max_bytes_per_sec": "200mb"
  }
}

Be careful when increasing these values. More concurrent recoveries and higher transfer rates put significant pressure on data nodes. If the infrastructure cannot handle the additional work, the nodes become overloaded, normal cluster operations suffer, and the entire cluster can become unresponsive.

I’ve experienced this firsthand: increasing recovery concurrency too aggressively overloaded the nodes and brought the cluster to a point where it stopped responding properly. Network saturation is another risk, especially when relocating large amounts of data between nodes.

Treat these values as temporary tuning, not recommended defaults. Increase them gradually, watch node and network utilization, and reduce them if the cluster shows signs of saturation. Once the migration is complete, restore the defaults by setting them to null:

PUT /_cluster/settings
{
  "persistent": {
    "cluster.routing.allocation.node_concurrent_recoveries": null,
    "indices.recovery.max_bytes_per_sec": null
  }
}

Which Downsize Pattern to Use

The right approach depends on the operation and on whether the disk survives the node:

Operation

EBS/EFS

Instance Store

Remove nodes (scale down)

Pattern 1: drain, then remove

Pattern 1: drain, then remove

Change the instance type (resize)

Rolling replacement that reattaches the volume, or Pattern 2

Pattern 2: Blue/Green

Pattern 1: Scale Down by Draining

Use this when you want fewer data nodes. It works for both network-attached storage (EBS, NFS) and ephemeral storage (Instance Store), because the node is empty before it is terminated.

Both patterns assume dedicated data nodes. If the nodes you are removing are also cluster-manager-eligible, removing several of them at once can break the cluster-manager quorum, so take them out of the voting configuration first.

Step 1: Check Capacity

Before draining, make sure the remaining nodes have enough free disk to absorb the shards you are about to relocate and still stay under the disk watermarks. Removing nodes puts the same data on fewer machines. If the remaining nodes fill past cluster.routing.allocation.disk.watermark.high, allocation stalls and you get stuck mid-scale-down. I explain how watermarks drive allocation in OpenSearch Shard Allocation: Balanced by Count, Rebalanced by Watermarks.

Use GET /_cat/allocation?v to compare the disk used on the nodes you are removing with the free disk on the nodes that stay.

Step 2: Disable Shard Rebalancing

Tell OpenSearch to stop moving shards around for balance:

PUT /_cluster/settings
{
  "persistent": {
    "cluster.routing.rebalance.enable": "none"
  }
}

This prevents background rebalancing from competing with the drain and wasting I/O and bandwidth on movements you are about to undo. Disabling rebalancing does not stop OpenSearch from moving shards off excluded nodes, so the drain in the next step still works.

Step 3: Drain the Nodes You Are Removing

Exclude the nodes from shard allocation before terminating them:

PUT /_cluster/settings
{
  "persistent": {
    "cluster.routing.allocation.exclude._name": "opensearch-data-4, opensearch-data-5"
  }
}

On Kubernetes, a StatefulSet scale-down always removes the pods with the highest ordinals. Going from six replicas to four removes opensearch-data-5 and opensearch-data-4, so those are the nodes to exclude.

OpenSearch now moves all primary and replica shards off the excluded nodes. Monitor progress with:

# look for `RELOCATING` or `UNASSIGNED` shards.
GET _cat/shards?v&s=state

# verify the excluded nodes are draining.
GET _cat/shards?v&s=node

# watch the recovery and relocation tasks.
GET _cat/tasks

# wait for green.
GET _cluster/health

Wait until the excluded nodes have zero shards assigned and the cluster is green before proceeding.

Step 4: Remove the Drained Nodes

Once the nodes are empty, remove them, for example by scaling the StatefulSet down, and confirm the cluster is still green afterward.

With EBS, scaling down does not delete the PersistentVolumeClaims of the removed pods by default. Their volumes keep costing money, and they reattach with stale data the next time you scale up. Delete them, or set the StatefulSet’s persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy so Kubernetes removes them on scale-down.

Step 5: Clear the Exclusion and Re-enable Rebalancing

Remove the exclusion and restore rebalancing:

PUT /_cluster/settings
{
  "persistent": {
    "cluster.routing.allocation.exclude._name": null,
    "cluster.routing.rebalance.enable": null
  }
}

Do not skip the exclusion cleanup. StatefulSets reuse pod names, so the next time you scale up, a new opensearch-data-4 would join the cluster still excluded and never receive shards. If you raised the recovery limits, restore them as well.

Pattern 2: Resize with Blue/Green Node Sets

Use this when you need to replace the nodes themselves, not just remove some of them. The typical case is changing the instance type of nodes whose disks do not survive replacement, such as NVMe SSDs on EC2 Instance Store. You cannot resize these nodes in place, because the new instance starts with an empty disk. The data has to move to the new node set before the old one goes away.

With network-attached storage the trade-off is different. On Kubernetes, an EBS-backed StatefulSet pod can move to a node with a different instance type and its volume reattaches. A rolling replacement then only has to recover the writes that happened while the pod was down. EBS volumes are bound to one Availability Zone, so the new node must run in the same zone as the volume. Blue/Green still works for EBS, but it copies the entire dataset.

The idea: run two StatefulSets in parallel (blue and green), migrate shards from one to the other, then decommission the old set. If you run the hot tier on Instance Store, the readiness probe and Karpenter settings from OpenSearch + EC2 Instance Store apply to both StatefulSets during this process.

Step 1: Disable Shard Rebalancing

Same as Pattern 1, prevent automatic redistribution while you are in control:

PUT /_cluster/settings
{
  "persistent": {
    "cluster.routing.rebalance.enable": "none"
  }
}

Step 2: Bring Up the New Node Set (Green) Without Data

Exclude the new nodes from shard allocation before they start, so they can boot and join the cluster without triggering a flood of shard movement. New indices, such as the next rollover, would otherwise be allocated to them right away:

PUT /_cluster/settings
{
  "persistent": {
    "cluster.routing.allocation.exclude._name": "green-node-1, green-node-2, green-node-N"
  }
}

Deploy the new node set and wait for all nodes to reach Ready status. The green nodes need the same node attributes as the blue ones, for example the attribute that marks them as hot tier. If your indices use index.routing.allocation.require.* filters and the green nodes lack the matching attribute, the shards have nowhere to go and the migration stalls.

Step 3: Migrate Data from Blue to Green

Now flip the exclusion to the old (blue) nodes. OpenSearch begins moving shards off the blue nodes and onto the green nodes:

PUT /_cluster/settings
{
  "persistent": {
    "cluster.routing.allocation.exclude._name": "blue-node-1, blue-node-2, blue-node-N"
  }
}

Monitor the migration closely:

# look for `RELOCATING` or `UNASSIGNED` shards.
GET _cat/shards?v&s=state

# verify the blue nodes are draining.
GET _cat/shards?v&s=node

# watch the recovery and relocation tasks.
GET _cat/tasks

# wait for green.
GET _cluster/health

Do not proceed until all shards have moved off the blue nodes and cluster health is green.

Step 4: Decommission the Old Node Set

Once all data is on the green nodes, delete the old (blue) StatefulSet:

kubectl delete sts <blue-statefulset-name>

This terminates every blue pod at once. That is safe for empty data-only nodes, but see the cluster-manager note in Pattern 1 if the blue nodes have other roles.

Step 5: Clean Up Exclusions and Restore Settings

Remove the exclusion rules so future shard assignments work normally, restore rebalancing, and reset the recovery limits if you raised them:

PUT /_cluster/settings
{
  "persistent": {
    "cluster.routing.allocation.exclude._name": null,
    "cluster.routing.rebalance.enable": null,
    "cluster.routing.allocation.node_concurrent_recoveries": null,
    "indices.recovery.max_bytes_per_sec": null
  }
}

Key Takeaways

  • Scaling down is riskier than scaling up because existing data must be relocated before nodes are removed.

  • Draining with exclude._name works for any storage type. Once a node is empty, losing its disk does not matter.

  • Resizing nodes on ephemeral storage requires Blue/Green. On EBS-backed StatefulSets, a rolling replacement that reattaches volumes is usually cheaper.

  • Disable shard rebalancing during planned migrations. It does not block the relocation of shards off excluded nodes.

  • Use persistent settings so a cluster restart does not silently drop your exclusions, and clear them afterward. StatefulSets reuse pod names, so a leftover exclusion will catch the next node with the same name.

  • Always verify shard allocation, cluster health, and available disk capacity before moving to the next step.

References

  • Cluster Settings API (OpenSearch)

  • Cluster settings reference (OpenSearch)

  • Cluster Allocation Explain API (OpenSearch)

  • Availability and recovery (OpenSearch)

  • CAT shards (OpenSearch)

  • StatefulSets (Kubernetes)

entry.title: OpenSearch + EC2 Instance Store: A Disruptive Approach to Hot Tier Storage
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2026/11/08

This blog post covers running the OpenSearch hot data tier on EC2 Instance Store (local NVMe) instead of EBS. It explains why local disks perform better for this workload, and how to manage the risk of data loss with OpenSearch replication, Kubernetes, and Karpenter.

Instance Store: Less Durability, More Performance

I’ve been managing OpenSearch clusters on EKS for over five years, handling ingestion rates of around 70K~100K documents per second. During this time, I’ve worked on improving indexing throughput, reducing query latency, and optimizing infrastructure costs. One of the most important changes was introducing hot, warm, and cold storage tiers to handle different data access patterns more efficiently. As the clusters grew, however, the hot tier became a performance bottleneck.

I experimented with different EC2 instance families and increased CPU and memory, but the metrics consistently pointed to storage I/O as the limiting factor. This led me to test Storage Optimized EC2 instances with local NVMe Instance Store for the hot data nodes. The results were very good: the local disks gave us the performance we needed and reduced storage costs compared with EBS.

There is an important trade-off, though. Instance Store disks are tied to the physical EC2 host. If an instance is stopped, terminated, or hits a host failure, its local data is permanently lost. That makes Instance Store less durable, but it does not make it unsuitable for OpenSearch. The key is understanding how shard replication works (I covered the basics in OpenSearch Concepts: Index and Shards) and designing the infrastructure so that losing a node never means losing the only copy of its data.

For more on performance, see these public benchmarks and case studies:

  • Tuning Your Cluster for Indexing Speed (by OpenSearch): Official OpenSearch guidance on indexing performance, including recommendations for SSD-backed Instance Store and storage configuration.

  • Postgres Isn’t Slow. Your Storage Is (by ClickHouse): Benchmark comparing EBS gp3 and local NVMe Instance Store using PostgreSQL workloads. Reports significant improvements in transaction throughput and latency with local NVMe.

  • Amazon EC2 i3.metal Review (by StorageReview): Storage benchmark comparing EBS and local NVMe on EC2 i3.metal instances, including random read/write IOPS and sequential throughput.

EC2 Instance Store vs. EBS

The difference comes down to where the disk is. An EBS volume is a network-attached block device that exists independently of any EC2 instance, so every I/O makes a network round trip. EC2 Instance Store is an NVMe SSD attached to the host’s PCIe bus, with no network in the path.

EBS (gp3)

Instance Store (local NVMe)

Attachment

Network-attached, independent of the instance

Physically attached to the host

Survives stop or terminate

Yes, and can be detached and reattached

No, the data is lost

Performance

3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s baseline, provisioned higher if needed and capped by the instance’s EBS bandwidth

Fixed by the instance type, with no network hop

Size

Chosen per volume, can grow

Fixed by the instance type, e.g. 1 x 1,875 GB on an i8g.2xlarge

Cost

Billed separately per GB-month, plus provisioned IOPS and throughput above the baseline

Included in the instance price

Local NVMe is not faster for every workload. For large sequential reads and writes, where most of the active data fits in RAM, a gp3 volume on an instance with enough EBS bandwidth can keep up with local drives, and the bottleneck becomes the instance’s EBS bandwidth rather than the disk.

Small random reads are where local NVMe clearly wins, because removing the network hop removes latency from every single I/O. This is the access pattern that matters for a search engine. When an OpenSearch hot tier serves queries against indices larger than the available RAM, Lucene has to read many small blocks from disk, and local storage answers those reads faster.

For most stateful applications, EBS remains the sensible default. In a distributed search system where shard replication already handles node failure, the durability EBS adds matters less, and local NVMe removes storage latency as the bottleneck.

Why Instance Store Works for OpenSearch

OpenSearch splits index data into shards and can keep replica copies of each shard on different data nodes. When a hot data node fails, its local NVMe data is gone, but if another node holds a valid copy of each affected shard, OpenSearch promotes those replicas to primary and allocates new replicas on the remaining nodes. Once a replacement node joins the cluster, it receives shard copies and the configured redundancy is restored.

This is what makes it possible to treat Instance Store disks as disposable, as long as every shard has another valid copy on a different node. The risk is losing several nodes that hold copies of the same shard before OpenSearch finishes recovering. So Instance Store is viable only when replication, placement, and node replacement are designed together. If you want more detail on how OpenSearch decides where shards go, see OpenSearch Shard Allocation: Balanced by Count, Rebalanced by Watermarks.

Running Instance Store Safely on Kubernetes

The following six mechanisms combine OpenSearch, Kubernetes, and Karpenter features to reduce the risk of data loss. They cover three areas: shard redundancy, workload placement, and controlled node replacement.

These mechanisms reduce risk during controlled operations, but they cannot guarantee durability. If multiple nodes fail before OpenSearch recovers their shard copies, data can still be lost. Using Instance Store means accepting that trade-off in exchange for performance. When durability is the priority, EBS remains the safer choice.

1. Ensure All Indices Have Replicas

Every index stored on Instance Store nodes needs at least one replica. Without replicas, a node failure can permanently remove the only copy of a shard. An index template can set a default replica count for new indices:

PUT /_index_template/default-replicas
{
  "index_patterns": ["*"],
  "template": {
    "settings": {
      "number_of_replicas": 1
    }
  }
}

This template only applies to new indices. Existing indices must be checked and updated separately, and explicit index settings or other templates with a higher priority can override it. Validate and monitor replica counts so that no index is left without redundancy.

2. Use StatefulSets for Hot Data Nodes

StatefulSets give each pod a stable identity and a predictable name, which helps when managing OpenSearch nodes that use local storage. With the default RollingUpdate strategy, Kubernetes replaces StatefulSet pods one at a time and waits for each updated pod to become Ready before moving to the next one. This prevents multiple hot data nodes from being replaced at the same time during an update.

Stable pod names are also useful when decommissioning or migrating nodes. For example, before removing opensearch-hot-3, you can ask OpenSearch to move its shards elsewhere by excluding it from shard allocation:

PUT /_cluster/settings
{
  "persistent": {
    "cluster.routing.allocation.exclude._name": "opensearch-hot-3"
  }
}

OpenSearch then relocates the shards away from the excluded node, and once relocation finishes, the node can be removed safely. This requires the OpenSearch node.name to match the pod name. After the operation, clear the exclusion setting so the node can receive shards again.

3. One Hot Data Pod per Worker Node

If two OpenSearch hot data pods run on the same Kubernetes worker, one EC2 failure takes down both, and they may hold the primary and the replica of the same shard. Running at most one hot data pod per worker keeps each EC2 instance a separate failure domain.

The following configuration uses pod anti-affinity to keep hot pods on separate Kubernetes nodes. You can combine it with node affinity to select dedicated hot-tier workers and topology spread constraints to distribute the pods across Availability Zones.

opensearch-data-hot-statefulset.yaml
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: opensearch-hot
    spec:
      affinity:
        # Ensure only one OpenSearch hot pod per Kubernetes node
        podAntiAffinity:
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
            - labelSelector:
                matchLabels:
                  app: opensearch-hot
              topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname

OpenSearch also supports shard allocation awareness, which tags nodes with their failure domain, such as the Availability Zone, so that OpenSearch places a shard’s copies in different zones. Keep in mind that cross-AZ traffic increases AWS data transfer costs.

4. Use a Readiness Probe to Wait for Cluster Green

An OpenSearch node that answers HTTP requests is not necessarily safe to move past. The process can be up before the cluster has recovered its shards and restored replica redundancy. A readiness probe that only checks the HTTP endpoint lets Kubernetes replace the next pod too early.

Instead, the probe can call the Cluster Health API and only report Ready when the cluster is green. Because the StatefulSet rolling update waits for each pod to be Ready, Kubernetes now waits for shard recovery before replacing the next pod. Set timeoutSeconds above the API’s own timeout; the default probe timeout is one second, which would make the probe fail while the request is still waiting:

opensearch-data-hot-statefulset.yaml
readinessProbe:
  timeoutSeconds: 10
  exec:
    command:
      - sh
      - -c
      - |
        curl -sSkf \
        -u "${USER}:${PASS}" \
        "${URL}/_cluster/health?wait_for_status=green&timeout=5s" \
        | jq -e '.status == "green" and .timed_out == false'

This check is cluster-wide. If any index turns yellow for an unrelated reason, every hot pod becomes NotReady at the same time, and Kubernetes removes all of them from the endpoints of any Service that selects them. Make sure clients reach the cluster through a Service that does not depend on this probe, such as one that points to coordinating nodes.

5. Use a PodDisruptionBudget (PDB)

A PodDisruptionBudget limits how many pods can be voluntarily evicted at the same time, for example while Kubernetes drains a worker node. The following PDB allows at most one hot data pod to be unavailable due to voluntary disruptions:

opensearch-data-hot-pdb.yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: opensearch-hot
spec:
  maxUnavailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: opensearch-hot

Choose maxUnavailable according to the cluster size, replica configuration, and failure tolerance. A limit of one is reasonable for many clusters, but it is not universally safe. A PDB also only covers evictions made through the Eviction API. It does not prevent involuntary failures, such as an EC2 instance interruption, and it does not control pod replacements made by a StatefulSet rolling update.

6. Control Node Disruptions with Karpenter

I’ll use Karpenter as an example, but the same logic applies to any node autoscaler.

Karpenter can replace nodes for several reasons, including consolidation and drift from the desired NodePool configuration. With Instance Store, terminating a node destroys its local data, so these replacements must be coordinated with OpenSearch shard recovery. Karpenter provides disruption controls for this.

One option is to add the karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt annotation to the pod template. Karpenter will not voluntarily disrupt a node running the annotated pod, subject to the documented exceptions:

opensearch-data-hot-statefulset.yaml
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt: "true"

Drift needs separate attention. When a node no longer matches its NodePool configuration, Karpenter may replace it, and for Instance Store hot nodes that means unplanned data movement and local data loss. A NodePool disruption budget set to zero for the Drifted reason stops Karpenter from voluntarily replacing drifted nodes:

opensearch-karpenter-nodepool.yaml
spec:
  disruption:
    budgets:
      - nodes: "0"
        reasons:
          - Drifted

When a node needs to be updated, adjust the budget to allow a controlled replacement, one node at a time. To replace or resize the whole hot tier, drain the shards off the old nodes first, as I describe in Scaling Down and Resizing OpenSearch Data Nodes Without Losing Data.

Each of these mechanisms covers a different kind of disruption. The readiness probe and the StatefulSet rolling update control the order of pod replacements during an update. The PDB limits voluntary evictions, such as Karpenter draining a node, but not StatefulSet-initiated replacements. The do-not-disrupt annotation and the NodePool budget stop Karpenter from replacing nodes on its own. None of them protects against unexpected infrastructure failures, such as an EC2 instance interruption.

Key Takeaways

  • Neither Instance Store nor EBS is better in general. EBS is durable and flexible; Instance Store trades durability for lower latency.

  • For an OpenSearch hot tier that serves queries on indices larger than RAM, the small random reads favor local NVMe.

  • Instance Store data is lost when the EC2 instance stops, terminates, or fails, so every index needs replicas.

  • Kubernetes and Karpenter guardrails (StatefulSet rolling updates, a green-cluster readiness probe, PDBs, anti-affinity, and disruption budgets) control planned replacements. Replication is what protects against unplanned ones.

References

  • Replica shards (OpenSearch)

  • Tuning for indexing speed (OpenSearch)

  • Cluster health API (OpenSearch)

  • Cluster awareness (OpenSearch)

  • Index templates (OpenSearch)

  • Storage optimized instances (AWS)

  • General Purpose SSD volumes (Amazon EBS)

  • StatefulSets (Kubernetes)

  • Configure a PodDisruptionBudget (Kubernetes)

  • Topology spread constraints (Kubernetes)

  • Disruption (Karpenter)

  • NodePools (Karpenter)

entry.title: OpenSearch Shard Allocation: Balanced by Count, Rebalanced by Watermarks
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2026/11/04

This blog post explains how OpenSearch distributes shards across data nodes. It covers how the default allocator works, why it can leave disk usage uneven in clusters with many small indices, and how disk watermarks correct that. It also covers other allocation mechanisms and a limitation I run into often: watermarks are one cluster-wide setting, even in clusters with different storage tiers.

Why Shard Balance Matters

Shard allocation is the process that decides which data node holds each shard. An index is split into shards, each one a Lucene index that holds part of the data, so indexing and search run in parallel across the cluster. That only works if data nodes have free disk space for new shards as indices are created and existing data grows.

If most of the free space is concentrated on a few nodes, the cluster can struggle to allocate new shards, even when there is plenty of storage in total.

When allocation fails, the cluster goes yellow or red. In a red state, at least one primary shard is unavailable, which can mean data loss if no recoverable copy exists. The GET /_cluster/allocation/explain endpoint shows why a shard was allocated to a node, or why an allocation or rebalance was rejected.

How OpenSearch Balances Shards Across Data Nodes

OpenSearch’s default shard allocator, BalancedShardsAllocator.java, uses a weighted balancing model. It considers both the total number of shards per node and how shards from each index are distributed across the nodes. The default weights are controlled by cluster.routing.allocation.balance.shard and cluster.routing.allocation.balance.index. Their default values are 0.45 and 0.55, respectively.

Shard size is not a factor in this balancing model. As a result, two nodes can have a similar number of shards while consuming very different amounts of disk space. That leads to surprises in production, especially in clusters with many small, granular indices. A node might hold dozens of tiny shards and use very little disk space, while another holds only a few large shards and is almost full. The shard distribution may look balanced, but disk usage tells a different story.

Allocation also respects other constraints, called allocation deciders: disk availability, allocation filters, awareness across availability zones or racks, and limits on shards per node. A decider can block an allocation even when it would improve the balance. The common allocators section of the documentation lists them.

Shard Allocation Mechanisms

The default allocator isn’t the only thing that influences shard placement. OpenSearch has other settings and APIs, although none of them replaces the default balancing strategy.

Load-Aware Allocation

Load-aware allocation limits how many shards can pile up on each node when the cluster loses capacity, for example when data nodes fail.

For example, consider a cluster with 10 data nodes and 100 shards, initially holding 10 shards per node. If 5 nodes fail, the remaining 5 nodes need to accommodate the 50 shards from the failed nodes. OpenSearch could redistribute all 50 shards across the surviving nodes, leaving each with around 20 shards: its original 10 shards plus 10 redistributed from the failed nodes.

Twice as many shards per node as planned can be a problem, depending on the node resources and workload. Load-aware allocation caps the shards per node based on the average shard count across the originally provisioned capacity, so the surviving nodes don’t get overloaded after a failure.

The following configuration sets the provisioned capacity to 10 nodes and defines how much shard concentration is allowed:

cluster.routing.allocation.load_awareness.provisioned_capacity: 10
cluster.routing.allocation.load_awareness.skew_factor: 50
cluster.routing.allocation.load_awareness.flat_skew: 2
cluster.routing.allocation.load_awareness.allow_unassigned_primaries: true

Here, provisioned_capacity remains 10, even after the failure, because it represents the intended cluster capacity. skew_factor allows 50% more shards than the original average of 10, while flat_skew adds 2 extra shards, bringing the limit to 17 per node.

With only 5 nodes available, each can hold up to 17 shards, so 85 of the 100 shards can be allocated. The remaining 15 shards stay unassigned until additional capacity becomes available. allow_unassigned_primaries controls whether primary shards can remain unassigned when the load-awareness limit prevents their allocation.

Manual Shard Allocation

The Cluster Reroute API, POST /_cluster/reroute, lets you move shards between nodes by hand, among other operations. For example, if node1 is running low on disk and node2 has plenty of free space, this request moves shard 0 of the logs-2026.11 index from node1 to node2. Add ?dry_run=true to simulate it first:

POST /_cluster/reroute
{
  "commands": [
    {
      "move": {
        "index": "logs-2026.11",
        "shard": 0,
        "from_node": "node1",
        "to_node": "node2"
      }
    }
  ]
}

The move still goes through the allocation deciders, so OpenSearch rejects it if the destination doesn’t have enough disk or breaks another constraint. The API is useful for one-off operations, but it doesn’t change the default strategy or add automatic size-based balancing. To move every shard off a node, an allocation exclusion is a better tool, as I show in Scaling Down and Resizing OpenSearch Data Nodes.

Balancing by Size: Disk Watermarks

Disk watermarks are thresholds of disk usage that change how OpenSearch allocates shards. There are three, low, high, and flood_stage, and each triggers a different action. They accept a percentage of each node’s disk or an absolute amount of free space. For example, consider a node with 1 TB of storage and this configuration:

cluster.routing.allocation.disk.watermark.low: 85%
cluster.routing.allocation.disk.watermark.high: 90%
cluster.routing.allocation.disk.watermark.flood_stage: 95%

When disk usage reaches 85%, the low watermark prevents OpenSearch from allocating new shards to that node, except for primary shards of newly created indices. At 90%, the high watermark triggers shard relocation attempts to nodes with more available disk space. If usage reaches 95%, the flood_stage watermark applies a read-only block to indices with shards on that node to prevent the disk from running out of space.

Shard balancing and disk watermarks complement each other. The default allocator keeps balancing by shard count and index distribution, while the disk threshold decider adds disk usage limits to its decisions.

Disk usage is not a continuous weight in the default allocator. It only starts to influence placement when a node crosses a watermark: low stops new shards from landing there, and high starts moving shards away. Together, the two mechanisms keep shards balanced while protecting disk capacity.

Watermark Limitation: One Setting For All Storage Tiers

There is one limitation in the watermark design that I find particularly frustrating: watermarks are global cluster settings. You configure them once, and the same thresholds apply to every node, regardless of its storage tier. That’s a problem in tiered clusters with hot, warm, and searchable nodes, such as the hot tier on EC2 Instance Store I run. Each tier has a different storage profile and a different cost per gigabyte. For example, a watermark that works well for warm nodes, where you want to use disk capacity efficiently before relocating shards, might be too aggressive for hot nodes. Hot nodes need more free space to handle indexing and query workloads. Yet OpenSearch gives you no way to configure different watermark thresholds for each tier.

Another scenario worth considering is OpenSearch Dashboards multi-tenancy. When multi-tenancy is enabled, each user has a private tenant with a dedicated index to store saved objects, such as visualizations, dashboards, and index patterns. Custom tenants also have their own indexes, while the global tenant is shared among users. In environments with many Dashboards users, this can result in a large number of small, granular indexes. Although each index may consume very little disk space, its shards still contribute to the total shard count considered by the default allocation strategy. That makes the shard distribution even less representative of real disk usage. The same happens when you create one small index per environment, which is why I replace per-environment indexes with filtered aliases.

I’d like to see per-tier watermark configuration in OpenSearch. Until that happens, we’re stuck with a single set of thresholds for the entire cluster. Keep this in mind when designing tiered clusters, because whatever values you choose will be a compromise across all storage tiers.

Key Takeaways

  • The default allocator balances by shard count and index distribution (balance.shard 0.45, balance.index 0.55). Shard size is not a factor.

  • With many small indices, nodes can have similar shard counts and very different disk usage.

  • Disk watermarks add size awareness: low stops new shards on a node, high moves shards away, and flood_stage puts a read-only block on indices with shards on the node.

  • Load-aware allocation caps shards per node after a capacity loss, based on the provisioned capacity, skew_factor, and flat_skew.

  • POST /_cluster/reroute moves individual shards, but it still goes through the allocation deciders.

  • Watermarks are global, so tiered clusters must use one compromise threshold for every tier.

  • GET /_cluster/allocation/explain shows why a shard was or wasn’t allocated.

References

  • NodeLoadAwareAllocationDecider.java (OpenSearch source)

  • ShardsAllocator interface (OpenSearch source)

  • Cluster settings (OpenSearch)

  • Cluster Settings API (OpenSearch)

  • Cluster Reroute API (OpenSearch)

  • Shard allocation filtering (OpenSearch)

  • Dashboards multi-tenancy: tenant indexes (OpenSearch)
