entry.title: Stop Extracting Metrics from OpenSearch Logs
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2026/11/03

This blog post explains why counting log lines in OpenSearch is an expensive way to produce a metric. The same number captured as a Prometheus counter is stored once and read almost for free. When you cannot change the application, Fluent Bit can extract that metric while the logs are ingested, so OpenSearch never has to rebuild it at query time.

How a Log Store Becomes a Metrics Database

For the past five years, I have worked on large OpenSearch deployments running on Kubernetes. One of the hardest problems was keeping query latency low while the volume of logs kept growing. I tried many performance optimizations, but the most useful step was a different question: how was the data actually being used?

In one case, the logs were not only stored for troubleshooting. Teams also queried them to find specific events and extract operational numbers, which made query latency critical and more expensive as ingestion grew. That taught me that tuning the infrastructure is only part of the answer. You also have to understand what the data is, how it is consumed, and which tool fits each use case.

It usually starts small. Someone needs a number, such as “how many payments failed in the last hour?”. The logs are already there, so they write a query that counts the matching log lines and pin it to a dashboard. It works. Then the dashboard gets slow, the log cluster runs hot, and the query that counts errors per minute starts timing out during an incident, when you need it most. The cause is rarely a bad query or an undersized cluster. Logs are being asked to do a metric’s job.

Logs and Metrics Are Different Shapes of Data

A log is a record of one event, written for a human (or an AI agent) to read. It is detailed, high-cardinality text:

2026-02-14T10:32:11Z level=error service=payments txn_id=8f3c user_id=22190 msg="payment authorization failed" provider=acme code=INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS latency_ms=812

The value of a log is its context. When something breaks, it tells you what happened, to whom, and often why. A log answers “walk me through this specific event.”

A metric is a number sampled over time. It is small, structured, and built to be aggregated:

payment_failures_total{provider="acme", code="INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS"} 48213

This metric does not describe one payment. It counts all of them, so it can be summed, rated, and broken down cheaply across huge volumes. A metric answers “how many, how fast, how much, right now and over time.”

Signal

What it is

Primary question

Natural shape

Logs

Discrete event records

“What exactly happened here?”

High-cardinality text

Metrics

Numeric samples over time

“How many / how fast / how much?”

Small numeric time series

When you ask a log store to answer the metric question, you force one shape of data to behave like the other. That is where the cost comes from.

Why Counting Log Lines Doesn’t Scale

OpenSearch is very good at full-text search. Its inverted index maps terms to the documents that contain them, so a question like “show me every error from payments mentioning acme yesterday” comes back fast. That is a search workload, and OpenSearch is the right tool for it.

Failed payments per minute is a different kind of question. As a log query, it looks like this:

GET my-app-logs-index-*/_search
{
  "size": 0,
  "query": {
    "bool": {
      "filter": [
        { "match": { "level": "error" } },
        { "match_phrase": { "msg": "payment authorization failed" } },
        { "range": { "@timestamp": { "gte": "now-24h" } } }
      ]
    }
  },
  "aggs": {
    "per_minute": {
      "date_histogram": {
        "field": "@timestamp",
        "fixed_interval": "1m"
      }
    }
  }
}

The query works, but look at what the cluster does to return one small time series:

  • The number is rebuilt on every read. No failures_per_minute value is stored anywhere, only the raw events. OpenSearch scans the matching documents and builds the count again each time the dashboard refreshes.

  • The cost follows the raw volume. To return 1,440 numbers (one per minute for a day), the cluster filters and buckets potentially millions of large text documents.

  • Breakdowns and long retention multiply the work. Splitting failures by provider and error code over 90 days fans the aggregation out across even more documents. You also have to keep verbose logs for 90 days only to keep a counter alive, long after they stopped being useful for debugging.

  • It competes with the real workload. These aggregations run on the same hot nodes that handle ingestion and incident searches, so the dashboard slows down the logging the cluster exists to serve.

OpenSearch has date histograms, aggregations, and dashboards, so it can do this. It is just not built for it. Counting term matches to produce a long-lived counter is a query-time reconstruction of data that was never stored as a measurement, and it gets worse as volume and retention grow.

The Same Number as a Prometheus Counter

The fix is to capture the number in the right shape from the start. Instead of logging a line and counting it later, the application increments a counter when a payment fails and exposes it to Prometheus:

from prometheus_client import Counter

payment_failures = Counter(
    "payment_failures_total",
    "Total number of failed payment authorizations",
    ["provider", "code"],
)

# in the failure path:
payment_failures.labels(provider="acme", code="INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS").inc()

The application serves this counter on a /metrics endpoint, and Prometheus scrapes it, every 15 seconds for example. The number is now the stored data: one running total per label combination. Because a counter only goes up, rate() turns it into failures per second over any window, grouped by any label, and it handles counter resets after a deploy. Failures per minute become a short, instant query:

# per-second rate of failures over the last 5 minutes, by provider and code
rate(payment_failures_total[5m])

# or per-minute, summed across providers
sum(rate(payment_failures_total[1m])) by (code) * 60

Here is what each system does for the same question:

Logs-as-metrics (OpenSearch)

Real metric (Prometheus)

Where the number lives

Reconstructed at query time

Stored directly as a time series

Data scanned per read

Millions of text documents

A handful of pre-aggregated samples

Cost scales with

Raw log volume + retention

Number of time series (tiny)

Breakdown by labels

Expensive aggregation fan-out

Native, free (by (code))

Retention for 90d of “rate”

Keep 90d of fat logs

Keep tiny numeric samples

Load during an incident

Heavy, competes with log search

Negligible

OpenSearch pays for a full-volume scan to see that failures are spiking. Prometheus pays almost nothing, because it reads the number instead of rebuilding it. If you instrument with OpenTelemetry instead of the Prometheus client, the idea is the same: the application emits the measurement.

Workaround: Extract the Metric at Ingestion With Fluent Bit

The counter in the application is the right answer, but sometimes you cannot touch the code. It may be a legacy service nobody wants to rebuild, a closed-source component, or a third-party app that only writes logs and will never expose /metrics. You still need the number.

The middle ground is not counting log lines in OpenSearch. It is turning the event into a metric inside the log pipeline, before the log reaches storage. The log shipper already sees every line, so it can match the lines that represent the event and increment a real counter on the spot. The log still goes to OpenSearch for investigation, and the metric is emitted next to it.

Fluent Bit does this with the log_to_metrics filter. It needs structured records, though. Without a parser, the tail input stores each line as a single string under log, so fields like msg, provider, and code do not exist yet. The sample log above is in logfmt, so the input uses a logfmt parser first. The filter then matches the event with a KEY REGEX rule and turns fields into labels. The prometheus_exporter output exposes the result:

fluent-bit.yaml
service:
  flush: 1
  log_level: info

parsers:
  - name: logfmt
    format: logfmt

pipeline:
  inputs:
    - name: tail
      path: /var/log/payments/*.log
      tag: payments.log
      # turn each logfmt line into a structured record (msg, provider, code, ...)
      parser: logfmt

  filters:
    # emit a counter every time a line denotes a failed payment
    - name: log_to_metrics
      match: payments.log
      tag: payment_metrics
      metric_mode: counter
      metric_name: payment_failures_total
      metric_description: "Total number of failed payment authorizations"
      # KEY REGEX: only the records that represent the event
      regex: 'msg ^payment authorization failed$'
      # turn record fields into metric labels, same breakdown you wanted
      label_field:
        - provider
        - code

  outputs:
    # logs still go to OpenSearch for investigation
    - name: opensearch
      match: payments.log
      host: opensearch
      port: 9200
      index: payments-logs

    # metrics are exposed for Prometheus to scrape
    - name: prometheus_exporter
      match: payment_metrics
      host: 0.0.0.0
      port: 9999

Prometheus scrapes the exporter and gets the same counter you would have written in the code. Fluent Bit prefixes the name with log_metric_counter_ by default:

$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9999/metrics
# HELP log_metric_counter_payment_failures_total Total number of failed payment authorizations
# TYPE log_metric_counter_payment_failures_total counter
log_metric_counter_payment_failures_total{provider="acme",code="INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS"} 48213

The number is computed once, as the log passes through, instead of on every dashboard refresh. OpenSearch keeps the raw logs for investigating a specific event, and the metric lives in a store that is cheap to query and cheap to retain. If you already run Fluent Bit in the cluster, this fits in the same pipeline that collects pod logs.

This is still a workaround. You are parsing text to decide what counts, so a change in the log format can silently break the counter, and the event has to be logged in the first place. A counter in the code carries business meaning that a regex on a log line can only approximate, so instrument the application whenever you can. When the source is out of reach, extracting the metric at ingestion is far better than hammering the log store with query-time aggregations.

Right Tool for Each Signal

None of this makes OpenSearch the wrong choice. For logs, it is a great tool, and the inverted index makes event search and investigation fast. The mistake is using it for a signal it was not built to carry.

Signal

Purpose-built tools

Why they fit

Logs

OpenSearch / Elasticsearch, Loki

Inverted index / label index tuned for text search over events

Metrics

Prometheus, Mimir, VictoriaMetrics

Time-series storage with cheap aggregation and rate math

You can force every signal into one system, but you end up with slow dashboards, bloated retention, and query-time hacks that approximate what a purpose-built engine does natively. There is no silver bullet in a telemetry architecture. The best architecture is the one where each signal lands in the tool shaped for it.

Part of getting there is organizational. Good observability is a partnership between teams. The application team instruments the code, because only the people who know the business logic know which events matter and which labels make a metric meaningful. The infrastructure team provides the pipelines that ingest, store, and expose each signal where it belongs. A payment_failures_total{code=...} counter carries business meaning that infrastructure cannot invent from the outside.

Key Takeaways

  • Logs describe individual events. Metrics are numbers sampled over time. Treat them as different kinds of data.

  • Counting log lines in OpenSearch rebuilds the number on every read, so the cost grows with raw log volume and retention.

  • Metric dashboards on the log cluster run on the same hot nodes that serve ingestion and incident searches.

  • A Prometheus counter stores the number once. rate() turns it into any per-second or per-minute view, grouped by any label.

  • When you cannot change the code, extract the metric at ingestion with Fluent Bit’s log_to_metrics filter. Parse the line first so the fields exist.

  • Ingestion-time metrics are a workaround: a log format change can break them silently. Instrument the application when you can.

  • Keep each signal in a tool built for it, and let the application team decide which events and labels matter.

References

  • Metric types (Prometheus)

  • Query functions: rate() (Prometheus)

  • Log to metrics filter (Fluent Bit)

  • Tail input (Fluent Bit)

  • Logfmt parser (Fluent Bit)

  • Prometheus exporter output (Fluent Bit)

entry.title: OpenTelemetry: A Framework for Decoupling Your Observability
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2026/10/29

This blog post explains what OpenTelemetry is and what it’s for, without the abstract definitions. It covers the problem it solves, why it shines in microservice architectures, the complexity it brings, and when a simpler setup, such as plain Prometheus, is the better choice.

Why OpenTelemetry Is Hard to Understand at First

When I started studying OpenTelemetry, I struggled to understand what it actually was. The official definition calls it “an open-source, vendor-neutral observability framework”. It’s accurate, but it didn’t help me. I kept asking: Is it a library I add to my code? A service I run? Something like Prometheus?

The answer is “a bit of each, and not a backend”. What finally made it click for me was looking at the problem first.

The Problem: Every Vendor Has Its Own Everything

Before OpenTelemetry, observing an application meant picking a vendor, and the vendor came with its own library for your code, its own agent to collect the data, and its own format to send it.

Imagine fifty services instrumented with the Datadog library, and the company decides to move to another tool. Every service has to be changed, tested, and redeployed, because the vendor is written into the code. That is vendor lock-in, and it’s the main problem OpenTelemetry removes.

What OpenTelemetry Is

OpenTelemetry is an open standard, with official tools, for producing and moving telemetry data: metrics, traces, and logs. People often call it OTel. It covers everything between your code and the backend, but not the backend itself. Storage and dashboards stay with whatever tool you choose.

In plain terms, it has three parts:

  • In your application: an API that your code calls to say what to measure, and an SDK that decides how to process and send it. Your code depends only on the API, so it never mentions a vendor.

  • On the wire: OTLP is the OpenTelemetry Protocol, one standard format for all telemetry, which most observability vendors accept.

  • In your infrastructure, optionally: the Collector is a service that receives the data and forwards it to one or more backends.

The Collector is not required. The SDK can send OTLP straight to any backend that accepts it, and changing that backend means changing the SDK’s exporter configuration, usually an environment variable, not your code. The Collector earns its place when you want one place, outside your services, to decide where the data goes and what happens to it on the way.

A comparison that helps developers: JDBC in Java, or the DB-API in Python. Your code talks to one standard interface, and the database behind it can be swapped. OpenTelemetry does the same for telemetry.

Where OpenTelemetry Shines: Microservices

OpenTelemetry pays off most in microservice architectures, where many services, written in different languages by different teams, work together on the same request.

A payment request might cross an API in Python, a fraud check in Java, and a gateway in Go. With OpenTelemetry, all of them instrument the same way, use the same attribute names, and pass the same request context to each other, so one trace follows the request across every service. When something fails, you can go from a latency spike on a dashboard to the exact request and the service that slowed it down, because metrics, traces, and logs can share that context: logs emitted through OpenTelemetry carry the trace ID, and metrics can point to sample traces.

That’s also where the Collector pays off, as the one place to apply rules for every service: remove sensitive data, drop noisy telemetry to control cost, add Kubernetes metadata, or send the same data to two backends during a migration.

The Cost: OpenTelemetry Is Not Simple

All of that comes with complexity. There are new concepts to learn (API, SDK, exporters, resources, context propagation), SDKs to configure in every service, and, once you adopt it, a Collector to deploy, scale, and monitor. The specification is large, and some parts are newer than others in some languages. It also takes agreement between teams: instrumentation only pays off when every service follows the same conventions.

For a large system, that cost is small next to what you gain. For a small one, it can be more machinery than the problem needs.

When You Don’t Need OpenTelemetry

Small and simple systems. If you run a monolith or a handful of services, in one language, with one backend you don’t plan to change, a Prometheus client library and a Prometheus server already solve the problem. The application exposes /metrics, Prometheus scrapes it, and you’re done. Add OpenTelemetry when the system grows into the problems it solves, not before.

Software you didn’t write. OpenTelemetry instrumentation is for your own applications, the business services where only your team knows which events matter, such as payments processed or orders failed. Off-the-shelf services such as Logstash, PostgreSQL, Redis, NGINX, or OpenSearch already expose their own metrics, through a monitoring API or a Prometheus exporter. That’s where plain Prometheus shines: scrape what the tool already provides, and don’t try to instrument it yourself. If you already run the Collector, its prometheus receiver can scrape those same endpoints, so they still don’t need any OpenTelemetry instrumentation.

My Take

OpenTelemetry isn’t something to adopt everywhere by default. It’s the right tool when you have many business services, several teams, and a real need to follow requests across them or to keep your options open on vendors. In that scenario, the separation it brings is what I value most: the application team says what to measure, and the platform team decides where the data goes, without either waiting on the other.

Key Takeaways

  • OpenTelemetry is an open standard plus tools for producing and moving telemetry. It is not a backend.

  • Your code depends only on its API and data travels over OTLP, so changing vendors means changing configuration, not code.

  • The Collector is optional. The SDK can export straight to a backend; add the Collector when you need central routing and processing.

  • It shines in microservices: many services, languages, and teams sharing one way to instrument and one trace per request.

  • It adds real complexity: new concepts, SDK configuration in every service, and possibly a Collector to operate.

  • For small, simple systems, a Prometheus client and a Prometheus server are enough.

  • Use it for your own business services. For off-the-shelf software such as Logstash or PostgreSQL, scrape the metrics they already expose with Prometheus.

  • OpenTelemetry concepts: components (OpenTelemetry)

  • OpenTelemetry Collector (OpenTelemetry)

  • Context propagation (OpenTelemetry)

  • Instrumentation and exporters (Prometheus)

  • OpenTelemetry project page (CNCF)

entry.title: Hacking Your Zsh Terminal with Custom Widgets
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2026/10/28

This blog post explains how to create custom Zsh widgets: shell functions bound to keyboard shortcuts through the Zsh Line Editor (ZLE). It’s the Zsh version of Hacking Your Bash Terminal with Custom Widgets, and it ends with the same widget that reruns the current command every two seconds.

Understand the Basics

ZLE (Zsh Line Editor) is the part of Zsh that handles command-line editing, the Zsh counterpart of GNU Readline in Bash. A ZLE widget is a function that ZLE runs when you press its key. You write a Zsh function, register it as a widget with zle -N, and bind it to a key with bindkey.

While a widget runs, ZLE gives it special parameters. The four main ones are:

  • BUFFER: the whole content of the command line.

  • CURSOR: the cursor position, as an offset into BUFFER.

  • LBUFFER: the part of the line left of the cursor.

  • RBUFFER: the part of the line right of the cursor.

Unlike Bash, Zsh gives you LBUFFER and RBUFFER directly, so inserting text at the cursor is as simple as LBUFFER+="text".

To see them in practice, create a function called debug-hook-variables that prints all four, register it, and bind it to Ctrl+x:

# zsh function for debugging reserved variables
function debug-hook-variables() {
  echo 
  echo ">>> BUFFER:   $BUFFER"
  echo ">>> RBUFFER:  $RBUFFER"
  echo ">>> LBUFFER:  $LBUFFER"
  echo ">>> CURSOR:   $CURSOR"
}

# register the function as a ZLE widget
zle -N debug-hook-variables

# check if "debug-hook-variables" are registered as widget
zle -al | grep debug-hook-variables

# define "Ctrl+x" shortcut for "debug-hook-variables" widget
bindkey '^X' debug-hook-variables

# list all widgets with shortcut defined
bindkey -L

Now type something at the prompt and press Ctrl+x. For example, with the cursor right after definitely, the output is:

$ definitely| maybe  # press `Ctrl+x`

>>> BUFFER:   definitely maybe
>>> RBUFFER:   maybe
>>> LBUFFER:  definitely
>>> CURSOR:   10

RBUFFER starts with the space after definitely, and CURSOR is 10 because definitely has 10 characters.

In the default emacs keymap, Ctrl+x is also the prefix of several built-in bindings, such as Ctrl+x Ctrl+e in many setups. Binding Ctrl+x alone replaces that prefix. If you use those bindings, choose another key.

Practical Example: Repeated Command Execution

Now a useful widget: an alternative to watch. watch runs its command in a new sh -c, so your aliases, such as kgp, aren’t available (see this Stack Overflow thread). This widget runs whatever is on the command line every two seconds when you press Ctrl+x, in your current shell, so aliases work.

function repeat-command-widget() {
  while true; do
    clear
    eval "$BUFFER"
    sleep 2
  done
}

zle -N repeat-command-widget
bindkey '^X' repeat-command-widget

To test it, type a command and press Ctrl+x:

kgp     
### press `Ctrl+x`
### stop execution by `Ctrl+c`

kgp runs every two seconds until you press Ctrl+c, just like watch "kubectl get pods".

How to Register the Widget

Built-in ZLE widgets only need a bindkey line. A custom widget also needs its function and the zle -N registration, so put all three in ~/.zshrc:

# ~/.zshrc

# define the function
function repeat-command-widget() {
  while true; do
    clear
    eval "$BUFFER"
    sleep 2
  done
}

# register funtion as a widget
zle -N repeat-command-widget

# define Ctrl+x to execute "repeat-command-widget" command
bindkey '^X' repeat-command-widget

The Ctrl+x shortcut is then available in every new Zsh session.

Where to Go From Here

Widgets turn any repetitive edit or command into one key press. Many Zsh plugins are widgets too: fzf binds its history, file, and directory search as ZLE widgets, and zsh-autosuggestions, which I use in my ZSH + Starship setup, works by wrapping the built-in ones.

Key Takeaways

  • ZLE is the Zsh line editor. A widget is a function that ZLE runs when you press its key.

  • Register a function as a widget with zle -N name, then bind it with bindkey '^X' name. Check it with zle -al and bindkey -L.

  • Inside a widget, BUFFER holds the command line, CURSOR the cursor offset, and LBUFFER and RBUFFER the text left and right of the cursor.

  • watch runs its command in a new shell, so aliases fail. A widget that evals $BUFFER in a loop runs in your shell, so they work.

  • Put the function, zle -N, and bindkey in ~/.zshrc.

References

  • Zsh Line Editor: zle and bindkey builtins (Zsh manual)

  • Zsh Line Editor: user-defined widgets and their parameters (Zsh manual)

  • watch (Linux man pages)

entry.title: Hacking Your Bash Terminal with Custom Widgets
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2026/10/25

This blog post explains how to create custom Bash widgets: Bash functions bound to keyboard shortcuts through the GNU Readline library. It continues GNU Readline: The Magic Behind Terminal Autocomplete, and ends with a widget that reruns the current command every two seconds.

Understand the Basics

A widget is a function bound to a key that runs while you are editing the command line. In Bash, you write a function and bind it to a shortcut with bind -x, documented with the other Bash builtins.

When Bash runs a function through bind -x, it sets some Bash variables for it. The two that matter most are:

  • READLINE_LINE: the whole content of the command line.

  • READLINE_POINT: the cursor position, as an offset into READLINE_LINE.

The function can read them, and if it changes them, Bash updates the command line when the function returns.

To see them in practice, create a function called debug-hook-variables that prints both, and bind it to Ctrl+x:

### bash function for debugging reserved variables
debug-hook-variables() {
  echo ">>> READLINE_LINE: $READLINE_LINE"
  echo ">>> READLINE_POINT: $READLINE_POINT"
}

### "\C-x" is the code for `Ctrl+x` shortcut
bind -x '"\C-x": debug-hook-variables'

Now type something at the prompt and press Ctrl+x. For example, with the cursor right after definitely, the output is:

$ definitely| maybe  # press `Ctrl+x`

>>> READLINE_LINE: definitely maybe
>>> READLINE_POINT: 10

definitely has 10 characters, so the cursor is at offset 10. Bash also sets READLINE_ARGUMENT and READLINE_MARK, but they’re only needed in more advanced widgets.

Ctrl+x is also the prefix of several default Readline bindings, such as Ctrl+x Ctrl+e to edit the command in your editor. Binding Ctrl+x alone replaces that prefix in the current session. If you use those bindings, choose another key.

Practical Example: Repeated Command Execution

Now a useful widget: an alternative to watch. watch runs its command in a new sh -c, so your aliases, such as kgp, aren’t available (see this Stack Overflow thread). This widget runs whatever is on the command line every two seconds when you press Ctrl+x, in your current shell, so aliases work:

repeat-command-widget() {
  while true; do
    clear
    eval "$READLINE_LINE"
    sleep 2
  done
}

bind -x '"\C-x": repeat-command-widget'

To test it, type a command and press Ctrl+x:

kgp     
### press `Ctrl+x`
### stop execution by `Ctrl+c`

kgp runs every two seconds until you press Ctrl+c, just like watch "kubectl get pods".

How to Register the Widget

Bindings to built-in Readline functions go in ~/.inputrc. A custom Bash widget is shell code, so the function and its bind -x go in ~/.bashrc:

# ~/.bashrc

repeat-command-widget() {
  while true; do
    clear
    eval "$READLINE_LINE"
    sleep 2
  done
}

bind -x '"\C-x": repeat-command-widget'

The Ctrl+x shortcut is then available in every new Bash session.

Where to Go From Here

Widgets let you turn any repetitive edit or command into a single key press. Zsh has the same idea with its own line editor, ZLE, and I show the Zsh version of this widget in Hacking Your Zsh Terminal with Custom Widgets. If you’d rather use ready-made widgets, fzf ships widgets for history, file, and directory search.

Key Takeaways

  • bind -x '"KEY": function' runs a Bash function when you press KEY.

  • Inside the function, READLINE_LINE holds the command line and READLINE_POINT the cursor offset. Changing them changes the command line.

  • watch runs its command in a new shell, so your aliases don’t work there. A widget that evals READLINE_LINE in a loop runs in your shell, so they do.

  • Built-in Readline bindings go in ~/.inputrc. Custom widgets are shell code, so they go in ~/.bashrc.

  • Ctrl+x is a prefix for default Readline bindings. Binding it alone replaces them.

References

  • Bash builtins: bind (GNU Bash manual)

  • Bash variables: READLINE_LINE and READLINE_POINT (GNU Bash manual)

  • bind (SS64)

  • watch (Linux man pages)

entry.title: GNU Readline: The Magic Behind Terminal Autocomplete
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2026/10/18

This blog post explains what GNU Readline is and how it powers the line editing, history navigation, and auto-completion you use every day in the terminal. It also shows the configuration I reach for the most: making the Up and Down arrows search your command history by prefix. It’s a small change that saved me a lot of keystrokes.

For a long time I thought certain terminal features were tied to the specific Linux distribution I was running. The more I used the terminal, the more curious I got about how it worked under the hood. Why would pressing Tab autocomplete a command on one machine and do nothing on another? Why did the Up arrow behave differently depending on where I was?

After some research, I understood that most of these behaviors are not the shell itself. They come from a library sitting underneath it: GNU Readline. Once I knew which component was responsible, configuring it became trivial.

What is GNU Readline

GNU Readline is a library that provides command-line editing, history navigation, search, and auto-completion to interactive terminal programs. As the Readline user manual describes, any program linked against it gets the same editing commands. It’s installed on most Linux distributions and used by many REPL-style programs you already know, such as bash, the python interactive shell, psql, and gdb.

A practical example: when you press TAB in Bash and the command gets autocompleted, that is Readline acting behind the scenes. The same happens with CTRL + R for reverse history search, CTRL + A to jump to the start of the line, and CTRL + E to jump to the end. Those are Readline functions that Bash exposes, which is why they also work in psql and the python shell.

.inputrc is the Readline configuration file. Readline reads it from ~/.inputrc, or from the system-wide /etc/inputrc. It can change the editor’s behavior and bind keys to built-in Readline functions or to macros. A macro inserts a string as if you had typed it.

In Bash, the bind builtin binds a key to a Readline function while the shell is running. It’s the runtime equivalent of editing .inputrc, and it can also list the current bindings.

These settings are useful beyond Bash. Any interactive program that uses the same Readline library can provide familiar line editing and history controls. Bash-specific shell functions are a separate case: they can be attached to keys with bind -x.

Practical Example: Searching History by Prefix

Here is the Readline configuration I use the most. By default, the Up and Down arrows walk through your history one entry at a time, in order. That gets tedious when you run the same family of commands with different arguments.

Imagine a history like this:

kubectl get pods
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get svc
vim templates/debug.yaml
tail -f /var/log/messages
kubectl describe pod foobar

If I want to recall a kubectl command, pressing Up forces me to cycle through tail and vim first. The arrows ignore what I already typed. I wanted something simpler: type a prefix, then use the arrows to walk only through the history entries that start with it.

Readline already ships the functions for that. They just aren’t bound to the arrow keys by default, and I really don’t understand why this isn’t the default on every distribution. Some, like Fedora and AlmaLinux, already configure similar Readline commands out of the box. It is extremely useful and requires no additional package installation.

The two functions are:

  • history-search-backward: search backward through history for the line starting with the text before the cursor.

  • history-search-forward: the same, but forward.

To bind them to the arrow keys, add this to your .inputrc:

~/.inputrc
set completion-ignore-case on
"\e[A": history-search-backward
"\e[B": history-search-forward

This binds:

  • Up Arrow (↑): history-search-backward

  • Down Arrow (↓): history-search-forward

The \e[A and \e[B are the escape sequences your terminal sends when you press Up and Down. The extra set completion-ignore-case on is a bonus: it makes Tab completion case-insensitive, which I find handy.

After editing .inputrc, reload it without restarting the shell:

bind -f ~/.inputrc

Now the behavior changes. With the same history as before, if I type kubectl and press Up, Readline walks only through the entries that start with kubectl:

# type this, then press the Up arrow:
kubectl

# first Up  -> kubectl describe pod foobar
# next Up   -> kubectl get svc
# next Up   -> kubectl get nodes
# next Up   -> kubectl get pods

The vim and tail lines are skipped entirely, because they do not start with kubectl. On an empty prompt with no prefix, the arrows behave exactly like before and walk the full history. You get the prefix search only when you ask for it.

Why It’s My Favorite Readline Setting

This is one of those tiny configurations that changes how the terminal feels once you get used to it. I have been using prefix search on the arrow keys for years, and going back to a machine without it is genuinely annoying. The best part is that it costs nothing: no package to install, no plugin, just three lines in .inputrc.

Readline can also save you time in the CNCF exams. Workstation Setup for Kubernetes Exams (CKA, CKAD & CKS) shows how I set up history search by prefix on the exam workstation. If you want to go beyond built-in functions and bind your own shell code to keys, Hacking Your Bash Terminal with Custom Widgets continues from here with bind -x.

Key Takeaways

  • Line editing, history navigation, and Tab completion in Bash come from GNU Readline, not from Bash itself.

  • Every program that uses Readline, such as psql and the python shell, shares the same key bindings and .inputrc settings.

  • ~/.inputrc (or /etc/inputrc) configures Readline. The bind builtin changes bindings at runtime, and bind -f ~/.inputrc reloads the file.

  • Bind "\e[A" to history-search-backward and "\e[B" to history-search-forward to make the arrows search history by the typed prefix.

  • With an empty prompt, the arrows still walk the full history, so you only get prefix search when you type a prefix.

  • set completion-ignore-case on makes Tab completion case-insensitive.

References

  • GNU Readline user manual (Case Western Reserve University)

  • history-search-backward (Readline manual)

  • history-search-forward (Readline manual)

  • bind (SS64)

entry.title: Vim for Kubernetes Certification Exams (CKA, CKAD & CKS)
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2026/07/15

This blog post covers the minimal Vim configuration and the editing techniques I use in the Linux Foundation Kubernetes certification exams. You don’t need to master Vim. A small set of commands is enough to edit YAML manifests much faster under exam conditions.

Vim: Less Mouse, More Efficiency

The exam workstation includes VSCodium (the free and open-source binaries of VS Code), but it isn’t practical during the exam. Every task is done on a remote node over SSH, where VSCodium isn’t available. The connection to the workstation also often has noticeable latency, which makes the mouse slow and unreliable. The less you rely on the mouse, the faster you edit. This is where Vim shines.

Vim is a modal text editor: you switch between modes, such as Normal mode for moving and editing with short commands and Insert mode for typing text. That is what makes it fast without a mouse. Practice the commands below in the simulation labs, such as Killer Shell, until they become muscle memory.

Vim Configuration

This configuration is intentionally minimal and tuned for Kubernetes YAML. Two-space indentation prevents invalid YAML, line numbers make it easy to jump to a line, syntax highlighting helps reading, and the cursor column highlight shows the indentation level.

~/.vimrc
set nu        " Show line numbers
set ai        " Preserve indentation while editing
set et        " Convert tabs into spaces
set ts=2      " Display tabs as two spaces
set sw=2      " Indent and unindent using two spaces
set sts=2     " Make Tab and Backspace use two-space indentation
set hls       " Highlight search matches
set cuc       " Highlight the current cursor column
syntax on     " Enable syntax highlighting

Avoid using set mouse=a due to the exam workstation’s high connection latency. Also, the clipboard settings clipboard+=unnamedplus,autoselect do not work on the exam workstations.

Each exam task is performed on a different remote node. Before starting a task, copy your local ~/.vimrc to the target question machine:

scp ~/.vimrc node01:~/.vimrc

Essential Editing Commands

These are the commands you’ll use most. They copy, delete, replace, and repeat edits without the mouse. Ctrl+y works in Insert mode; the others run from Normal mode:

o           # Open a new line below
Shift+o     # Open a new line above
i           # Enter Insert mode
Shift+a     # Enter Insert mode at the end of the line
cW          # Cut the word under the cursor and enter Insert mode (for word replacement)
Shift+c     # Cut to the end of the line and enter Insert mode (for line replacement)
Ctrl+y      # Copy the character from the line above

y           # Yank (copy)
p           # Paste below
Shift+p     # Paste above
dd          # Cut the current line
dG          # Cut to the end of the file
dgg         # Cut to the beginning of the file

u           # Undo
Ctrl+r      # Redo

Shift+v     # Enter Visual Line mode (for indentation and copying)
Ctrl+v      # Enter Visual Block mode (for commenting lines)
>           # Indent to the right
<           # Indent to the left
.           # Repeat the last command
~           # Toggle character case

:retab      # Convert tabs to spaces
:wq         # Save and quit (or ZZ)

Cursor Movement

I strongly recommend not using set mouse=a in the exam. The remote exam workstations have higher latency than the Killer Shell simulator, so mouse interactions in Vim are slow and unreliable. Use the mouse only to scroll, and navigate with these commands:

/greeting   # Search for "greeting"
/foo/bar    # Search for "foo/bar"
n           # Jump to the next match
N           # Jump to the previous match
12gg        # Jump to line 12
0           # Jump to the beginning of the line
gg          # Jump to the beginning of the file
G           # Jump to the end of the file
W           # Jump to the next word
B           # Jump to the previous word

YAML Indentation

Indentation mistakes are one of the most common causes of invalid Kubernetes manifests. Vim indents whole YAML blocks to the right or left while keeping their structure.

To increase the indentation:

Shift+v   # 1. Select lines in Visual Line mode (↑↓)
>         # 2. Shift indentation to the right
ESC       # 3. Apply the change
.         # 4. Repeat the indentation

If you need to reverse the indentation or perform another operation on the same lines, use gv to restore the previous Visual selection:

gv      # 1. Reselect the previous Visual selection
<       # 2. Shift indentation to the left
ESC     # 3. Apply the change
.       # 4. Repeat the operation

Commenting Multiple Lines

Visual Block mode selects a rectangle of text across several lines, so you can insert the same text on all of them at once. It’s the quickest way to comment or uncomment a YAML block.

Ctrl+v    # 1. Select columns across lines in Visual Block mode (↑↓)
Shift+i   # 2. Enter Insert mode
#         # 3. Type the comment character
ESC       # 4. Apply the change to all selected lines

The same technique can also be used to insert identical text across multiple lines, such as prefixes, labels, or environment variables.

Search and Replace

When you rename resources, labels, namespaces, image names, or environment variables, replacing every occurrence by hand is slow and error-prone.

To replace every occurrence of a string:

:%s/foo/bar/g                   # Replace "foo" with "bar"
:%s#/kubernets/#/kubernetes/#g  # Replace "/kubernets/" with "/kubernetes/"

Sometimes you want to replace one occurrence at a time instead. Use this workflow:

*         # Search for the word under the cursor (or use "/greeting")
cW        # Replace the current occurrence
foobar    # Type the replacement text
n         # Jump to the next match
.         # Repeat the replacement
n         # Jump to the next match
n         # Skip this match and jump to the next one
Shift+n   # Go back to the previous match
.         # Repeat the replacement here

This approach lets you review each occurrence before replacing it, making it safer than a global search-and-replace.

Working with YAML Blocks

Many operations work directly on a range of line numbers, without Visual mode. That’s especially useful to move, copy, delete, or reindent large YAML blocks.

:%<         # Unindent all lines
:10,15>     # Indent lines 10-15
:10,15<     # Unindent lines 10-15
:30,50t70   # Copy lines 30-50 and paste below line 70
:30,50m70   # Cut lines 30-50 and paste below line 70
:30,50d     # Cut lines 30-50
:10,15y     # Copy lines 10-15
:50put      # Paste lines below line 50

Working with Numbers

Kubernetes manifests are full of numbers such as replica counts, ports, resource requests and limits, and probe timings. Instead of deleting and retyping them, Vim can increment or decrement them in place.

Place the cursor before or on a number, then use Ctrl+a to increment it or Ctrl+x to decrement it. You can also provide a count to change the value by a larger amount:

50 » Ctrl+a     # Increment the next number by 50
40 » Ctrl+x     # Decrement the next number by 40

For example, with the cursor on replicas:

replicas: 3

Pressing Ctrl+a changes it to:

replicas: 4

Likewise, 10 » Ctrl+a changes it from 3 to 13.

Running Shell Commands in Vim

Vim can pipe the file, or part of it, through any command-line tool and replace it with the output. For example, run yq on the whole buffer to catch syntax errors and format the file:

:%!yq

You can also apply the same approach to a selection of lines. For example, to sort and remove duplicate lines, select the lines and pipe them through sort and uniq:

Shift+v         # 1. Select lines in Visual Line mode (↑↓)
:!sort | uniq   # 2. Sort and remove duplicates from the selection

Vim can also execute commands without modifying the current buffer. This is useful when you need to quickly inspect information from the cluster while editing a manifest. For example, when editing a NetworkPolicy, you can check pod and namespace labels with:

:!kubectl get pods,ns --show-labels -n foobar

Another useful trick is saving a protected file you opened without sudo. When you’ve already made several changes, you don’t need to reopen it with sudo vim and repeat them. Write the buffer through sudo instead:

:w !sudo tee %

:w normally writes the buffer to a file. Followed by !, it sends the buffer’s content to a command’s standard input instead. Here, tee runs as root and writes it to %, the current file name.

Learn More

The Vim cheat sheet has many more commands, and the official Vim documentation covers each one in detail. To practice in exam conditions, use the simulator sessions that come with your exam registration.

For the rest of my exam workstation setup, including Bash aliases and history search by prefix, see Workstation Setup for Kubernetes Exams (CKA, CKAD & CKS). History search by prefix comes from GNU Readline, which I explain in GNU Readline: The Magic Behind Terminal Autocomplete.

Key Takeaways

  • Use Vim on the question nodes: VSCodium isn’t available there, and latency makes the mouse unreliable.

  • Keep ~/.vimrc minimal for YAML: line numbers, auto-indent, two-space tabs, and a cursor column highlight. Copy it to each node with scp.

  • Indent blocks with Shift+v, > or <, and repeat with .. Use gv to reselect the last selection.

  • Comment several lines with Ctrl+v, Shift+i, #, then ESC.

  • Replace globally with :%s/old/new/g, or one match at a time with *, cW, n, and ..

  • Use line ranges such as :30,50d, :30,50t70, and :30,50m70 to delete, copy, and move YAML blocks.

  • Change numbers with Ctrl+a and Ctrl+x, filter text through tools with :%!yq, and save a protected file with :w !sudo tee %.

References

  • Vim cheat sheet (vim.rtorr.com)

  • Vim help files (vimhelp.org)

  • Options: cursorcolumn (Vim documentation)

  • yq (GitHub)

  • sort (Linux man pages)

I’m Carlos Neto, and this blog is where I share my experiences and open source contributions. More about me on my home page. If you have questions or a different approach, contact me on LinkedIn.

entry.title: Workstation Setup for Kubernetes Exams (CKA, CKAD & CKS)
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2026/07/09

This blog post covers the workstation tweaks I use to work faster during the Linux Foundation Kubernetes exams: macOS settings that avoid keyboard and proctoring problems, Bash history search by prefix, a minimal Vim configuration, kubectl aliases, and how to copy all of it to each question node.

Time management is one of the most important factors for passing these exams. The CKA, CKAD, and CKS are hands-on exams that run on remote Ubuntu instances with the XFCE desktop, where network latency and the remote desktop slow you down. Every keystroke you save adds up.

Configure the U.S. Keyboard Layout (MacBooks)

If you take the exam on a MacBook, set your keyboard layout to U.S.. Otherwise, the remote Linux environment may not recognize some characters correctly, especially ~ and `. This is a common problem with layouts such as U.S. International - PC and Brazilian ABNT2.

Before the exam:

  1. Open System Settings » Keyboard » Input Sources.

  2. Add the U.S. input source.

  3. Remove all other input sources, so only U.S. remains.

Disable Mission Control Shortcuts (MacBooks)

By default, CTRL + ←→ switches between macOS Spaces. During the exam, the proctor can see that as leaving the exam environment, which may trigger a warning or even interrupt your session.

Before the exam:

  1. Open System Settings » Keyboard » Keyboard Shortcuts.

  2. Select Mission Control.

  3. Disable every shortcut under Mission Control.

That prevents accidental desktop switches and the risk of a proctor alert or a suspension on suspicion of consulting unauthorized material.

Disable Window Tiling Apps (MacBooks)

If you use a window tiling app such as Rectangle or Magnet, close it before the exam. Its keyboard shortcuts can conflict with the exam workstation and cause unexpected behavior with shortcuts such as ⌘ + ↑↓←→.

History Search by Prefix

This is my most valuable tip.

The exam environment uses Bash, and Bash relies on the GNU Readline library for command-line editing, key bindings, and history navigation. For example, the reverse search on CTRL + R comes from Readline. I explain how Readline works in more depth in GNU Readline: The Magic Behind Terminal Autocomplete.

History search by prefix is a Readline feature, disabled by default, that searches your history using the text already typed before the cursor. The history-search-backward and history-search-forward functions implement it, instead of simply moving to the previous or next command.

For example, imagine your command history contains:

kubectl get pods
kubectl get nodes
kubectl describe pod nginx
helm list

If you type:

kubectl g

and press ↑, history-search-backward cycles only through commands that start with kubectl g:

kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods

kubectl describe pod nginx and helm list are skipped because they don’t match the prefix. That’s much faster than the default ↑, which walks through every command, and often more convenient than pressing CTRL + R repeatedly.

To enable it, create ~/.inputrc with this configuration:

~/.inputrc
# ↑ (previous matching command)
"\e[A": history-search-backward
# ↓ (next matching command)
"\e[B": history-search-forward

Bash reads this file when a new session starts. To load changes in the current session, run:

bind -f ~/.inputrc

Setting Up Vim

The exam workstation includes VSCodium, but every task requires you to connect to a remote node over SSH, and VSCodium isn’t available there. The workstation also often has high latency, which makes the mouse unreliable. This is where Vim shines.

These settings make editing Kubernetes YAML manifests much easier. Create ~/.vimrc with:

~/.vimrc
set nu        " Show line numbers
set ai        " Preserve indentation while editing
set et        " Convert tabs into spaces
set ts=2      " Display tabs as two spaces
set sw=2      " Indent and unindent using two spaces
set sts=2     " Make Tab and Backspace use two-space indentation
set hls       " Highlight search matches
set cuc       " Highlight the current cursor column
syntax on     " Enable syntax highlighting

Avoid set mouse=a, because of the latency. Also, clipboard settings such as clipboard+=unnamedplus,autoselect don’t work on the exam workstations.

I wrote a separate post, Vim for Kubernetes Certification Exams (CKA, CKAD & CKS), with the editing techniques I use most during the exams.

kubectl Aliases and Shortcuts

Each remote question node already has a ~/.bashrc with useful settings. A handy trick is to copy it to the main workstation, append your own aliases, and copy it back to the question nodes.

First, copy ~/.bashrc from a question node:

scp cks1234:~/.bashrc ~/.bashrc

Then append these aliases to the end of the file:

~/.bashrc
### omitted the .bashrc copied from question node

alias kgp="kubectl get pods"

alias kaf="kubectl apply -f"
alias kdel="kubectl delete --now"
alias kdelp="kubectl delete pod --now"

alias kns="kubectl config set-context --current --namespace"
alias kctx="kubectl config use-context"

export x="--dry-run=client -oyaml"

INFO: export x is a shorthand to generate YAML from imperative kubectl commands, such as k run nginx --image nginx:latest $x > nginx.yaml.

I use the same style of aliases every day through the oh-my-zsh kubectl plugin, as I describe in ZSH + Starship.

Copy the Settings to Each Question Node

Every task must be done on a remote question node over SSH. Create your configuration files once on the main workstation, then copy them to the question node before you start each task:

scp ~/.inputrc ~/.vimrc ~/.bashrc cks1234:~/
ssh cks1234

Key Takeaways

  • On a MacBook, use only the U.S. keyboard layout, disable Mission Control shortcuts, and close window tiling apps before the exam.

  • Bind ↑ and ↓ to history-search-backward and history-search-forward in ~/.inputrc to search history by prefix.

  • Use Vim on the question nodes, with a small ~/.vimrc for YAML: line numbers, auto-indent, and two-space tabs.

  • Don’t enable set mouse=a or clipboard settings. They don’t help on the exam workstation.

  • Copy the question node’s ~/.bashrc, append your kubectl aliases and export x="--dry-run=client -oyaml", and copy everything back with scp before each task.

  • Vim cheat sheet (vim.rtorr.com)

entry.title: Helm Tips: Inspect Your Chart Context with JSON
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2026/02/25

This blog post shows a simple way to debug Helm charts: dump the entire chart context as JSON and look at exactly what your templates can access. It helps most when $ helm template fails with a message that doesn’t point to the real problem, such as a typo in a .Values path.

Debugging Helm charts is frustrating at first, especially if you come from programming languages with debuggers and IDE auto-completion. A template that reads a wrong .Values key, because of a typo or a wrong nesting level, often fails with an error far from the root cause.

Are There IDEs for Helm Charts?

Unfortunately, there is no IDE built for Helm. VS Code and JetBrains IDEA have plugins with some auto-completion, but nothing close to what you get with languages such as Python and Java.

I use VS Code with Kubernetes (by Microsoft) and YAML (by Red Hat). They help avoid typos in .Values and show the available Go template functions, but some variables are missing from auto-completion. I also tried the JetBrains Helm plugin, but it didn’t work as smoothly as the animation on its page suggests, and the Kubernetes plugin requires an IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate subscription.

Dump the Chart Context as JSON

Since the tooling falls short, I use another approach: render the whole Helm chart context as JSON. The chart context is the root object (.) that every template receives. It holds .Values, the chart and subchart metadata, release information, cluster capabilities, and the chart’s files.

First, create a chart called foobar and enter its directory:

helm create foobar
cd foobar

Then create a template named debug.yaml:

vim templates/debug.yaml

With this content. toPrettyJson is a template function that converts any object to indented JSON:

{{ . | toPrettyJson }}

Now render only that template. helm template with -s (--show-only) renders a single file, tail -n +3 drops the --- separator and the # Source: comment that Helm adds, and jq formats the result:

helm template -s templates/debug.yaml . | tail -n +3 | jq

A few things stand out in this output. For example, Capabilities.APIVersions lists the APIs you can check with .Capabilities.APIVersions.Has, Chart shows the metadata from Chart.yaml with Go-style capitalized names, and Files holds the content of every non-template file in the chart, base64-encoded in this dump.

Inspect Only What You Need

The full context is long. To focus on one part, pipe only that object to toPrettyJson. For example, to see the merged values after applying a values file:

{{ .Values | toPrettyJson }}

This is the fastest way I know to check what a chart actually receives after values files, --set flags, and subchart values are merged.

Remove the Debug Template When You Are Done

debug.yaml is a regular template, so helm install and helm upgrade would render it too, and its JSON is not a valid Kubernetes manifest. Delete it after debugging, or keep it out of the release with a condition such as {{- if .Values.debug }}.

If you’re designing a chart from scratch, Helm Charts: Development Practices from a Programmer’s Perspective covers how I decide what to template and what not to. I also template Logstash pipelines with Helm, as I show in Logstash DB Enrichment.

Key Takeaways

  • Helm has no real debugger, and IDE plugins only partly auto-complete chart variables.

  • {{ . | toPrettyJson }} in a template renders the whole chart context as JSON.

  • helm template -s templates/debug.yaml . | tail -n +3 | jq renders only that template and formats the output.

  • The context has Values, Chart, Release, Capabilities, Files, Subcharts, and Template.

  • Dump .Values alone to check the final merged values after values files and --set.

  • Delete the debug template, or guard it with a condition, before installing the chart.

entry.title: groupby + attrgetter: The Pythonic Way to Group Objects
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2025/07/28

This blog post shows how to group objects by several attributes. It uses two standard library tools, itertools.groupby and operator.attrgetter, instead of building a dictionary of lists by hand. It also covers the one detail that trips most people up: groupby only groups items that are next to each other.

The Example Data

To illustrate, here is a Band dataclass and a bands list. The goal is to group the bands by category, genre, and country, and print the names in each group.

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Band:
    name: str
    category: str
    genre: str
    country: str

bands = [
    Band(name="The Beatles", category="Rock", genre="Rock", country="UK"),
    Band(name="Queen", category="Rock", genre="Rock", country="UK"),
    Band(name="The Rolling Stones", category="Rock", genre="Rock", country="UK"),
    Band(name="Led Zeppelin", category="Rock", genre="Rock", country="UK"),
    Band(name="The Who", category="Rock", genre="Rock", country="UK"),
    Band(name="Deep Purple", category="Rock", genre="Rock", country="UK"),
    Band(name="Nirvana", category="Rock", genre="Grunge", country="USA"),
    Band(name="Temple of the Dog", category="Rock", genre="Grunge", country="USA"),
    Band(name="Pearl Jam", category="Rock", genre="Grunge", country="USA"),
    Band(name="Soundgarden", category="Rock", genre="Grunge", country="USA"),
    Band(name="Alice in Chains", category="Rock", genre="Grunge", country="USA"),
    Band(name="Stone Temple Pilots", category="Rock", genre="Grunge", country="USA"),
    Band(name="Pink Floyd", category="Rock", genre="Progressive Rock", country="UK"),
    Band(name="Genesis", category="Rock", genre="Progressive Rock", country="UK"),
    Band(name="Yes", category="Rock", genre="Progressive Rock", country="UK"),
    Band(name="King Crimson", category="Rock", genre="Progressive Rock", country="UK"),
    Band(name="The Smiths", category="Rock", genre="Indie Rock", country="UK"),
    Band(name="Arctic Monkeys", category="Rock", genre="Indie Rock", country="UK"),
    Band(name="Pet Shop Boys", category="Pop", genre="Synth-pop", country="UK"),
    Band(name="Depeche Mode", category="Pop", genre="Synth-pop", country="UK"),
    Band(name="Erasure", category="Pop", genre="Synth-pop", country="UK"),
    Band(name="Korine", category="Pop", genre="Synth-pop", country="USA"),
    Band(name="Oasis", category="Rock", genre="Britpop", country="UK"),
    Band(name="Blur", category="Rock", genre="Britpop", country="UK"),
    Band(name="Pulp", category="Rock", genre="Britpop", country="UK"),
    Band(name="Echo & the Bunnymen", category="Rock", genre="Post-Punk", country="UK"),
    Band(name="Joy Division", category="Rock", genre="Post-Punk", country="UK"),
    Band(name="The Cure", category="Rock", genre="Post-Punk", country="UK"),
    Band(name="The Killers", category="Rock", genre="Alternative Rock", country="USA"),
    Band(name="R.E.M.", category="Rock", genre="Alternative Rock", country="USA"),
    Band(name="Radiohead", category="Rock", genre="Alternative Rock", country="UK"),
    Band(name="U2", category="Rock", genre="Rock", country="Ireland"),
]

The Usual Approach: A Dictionary of Lists

The most common approach is a temporary dictionary whose key is a tuple of the grouping attributes and whose value is the list of objects that share them:

bands_groupby_genre_country = {}

for band in bands:
    group_key = (band.category, band.genre, band.country)
    bands_groupby_genre_country.setdefault(group_key, []).append(band)

for (category, genre, country), band_group in bands_groupby_genre_country.items():
    print(f">>> {category=}, {genre=}, {country=}:")
    for band in band_group:
        print(f"- {band.name}")

It works, but the intent is buried in the bookkeeping: create the dictionary, build the key, append to the list, then loop again to read it.

groupby With a Lambda

itertools.groupby is a standard library function that walks an iterable and yields one (key, group) pair for each run of consecutive items with the same key. It takes the iterable as its first argument and an optional key function. The key works exactly like the one in sorted: it is called for each item to compute the value to group by. In this example, a lambda returns the category, genre, and country of each band:

from itertools import groupby

attribute_group = lambda item: (item.category, item.genre, item.country)

for (category, genre, country), group in groupby(bands, key=attribute_group):
    print(f">>> {category=}, {genre=}, {country=}:")
    for band in group:
        print(f"  - {band.name}")

This already reads better: the loop says what it groups by and what it does with each group.

groupby With attrgetter

operator.attrgetter returns a callable that reads the given attribute from its argument. With several attribute names, it returns a tuple of their values. For this purpose it does the same job as the lambda, but the code says what it does without the extra syntax:

from operator import attrgetter
from itertools import groupby

attribute_group = attrgetter("category", "genre", "country",)

for (category, genre, country), group in groupby(bands, key=attribute_group):
    print(f">>> {category=}, {genre=}, {country=}:")
    for band in group:
        print(f"  - {band.name}")

The output is:

>>> category='Rock', genre='Rock', country='UK':
- The Beatles
- Queen
- The Rolling Stones
- Led Zeppelin
- The Who
- Deep Purple

>>> category='Rock', genre='Grunge', country='USA':
- Nirvana
- Temple of the Dog
- Pearl Jam
- Soundgarden
- Alice in Chains
- Stone Temple Pilots

>>> category='Rock', genre='Progressive Rock', country='UK':
- Pink Floyd
- Genesis
- Yes
- King Crimson

>>> category='Rock', genre='Indie Rock', country='UK':
- The Smiths
- Arctic Monkeys

>>> category='Pop', genre='Synth-pop', country='UK':
- Pet Shop Boys
- Depeche Mode
- Erasure

>>> category='Pop', genre='Synth-pop', country='USA':
- Korine

>>> category='Rock', genre='Britpop', country='UK':
- Oasis
- Blur
- Pulp

>>> category='Rock', genre='Post-Punk', country='UK':
- Echo & the Bunnymen
- Joy Division
- The Cure

>>> category='Rock', genre='Alternative Rock', country='USA':
- The Killers
- R.E.M.

>>> category='Rock', genre='Alternative Rock', country='UK':
- Radiohead

>>> category='Rock', genre='Rock', country='Ireland':
- U2

Sort Before You Group

There is one catch. As the itertools documentation says, groupby starts a new group every time the key changes. It only groups items that are next to each other. The bands list above is already ordered by group, which is why the output looks right. For example, if two UK rock bands were separated by a grunge band, they would end up in two different groups with the same key.

The dictionary approach doesn’t have this problem, because it looks up the key for every item. For groupby, sort the data by the same key first:

from operator import attrgetter
from itertools import groupby

attribute_group = attrgetter("category", "genre", "country")

for (category, genre, country), group in groupby(sorted(bands, key=attribute_group), key=attribute_group):
    print(f">>> {category=}, {genre=}, {country=}:")
    for band in group:
        print(f"  - {band.name}")

Reusing the same attrgetter for sorted and groupby keeps the two keys identical. Sorting changes the order of the groups, so the output is in alphabetical order of category, genre, and country.

For the full working example, see the GitHub repository. You can also run it directly in your terminal:

curl -s https://raw.githubusercontent.com/c-neto/my-code-playground/refs/heads/main/blog-code-examples/2025-07-28-groupby/python-groupby-example.py | python -

If you like small standard library tricks like this, Dynaconf covers the other side of Python services I write often: configuration. And for instrumenting a Python application, see OpenTelemetry: A Framework to Decoupling Your Observability.

Key Takeaways

  • A dictionary of lists works for grouping, but the intent gets lost in the bookkeeping.

  • itertools.groupby(iterable, key=...) yields one (key, group) pair per run of consecutive items with the same key.

  • operator.attrgetter("a", "b", "c") builds the grouping key as a tuple, with no lambda.

  • groupby only groups adjacent items, so sort with the same key first: groupby(sorted(items, key=k), key=k).

  • Both functions are in the standard library, so there is nothing to install.

References

  • itertools.groupby (Python documentation)

  • operator.attrgetter (Python documentation)

  • Key functions (Python Sorting HOW TO)

  • Lambda expressions (Python tutorial)

  • Full example for this post (GitHub)

I’m Carlos Neto, and this blog is where I share my experiences and open source contributions. More about me on my home page. If you have questions or a different approach, contact me on LinkedIn.

entry.title: Kubernetes Logs Simplified: Everything You Need to Know About Pod Logging
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2025/06/22

This blog post explains where Kubernetes stores container logs and how $ kubectl logs and log shippers read them. It also covers the CRI log line format, how log rotation works, and how to ship pod logs to an external system with a DaemonSet. Kubernetes logging can look complex, but knowing these details makes troubleshooting much easier.

How Kubernetes Stores Container Logs

Kubernetes runs containers through a container runtime, such as containerd or CRI-O. The Container Runtime Interface (CRI) is the API that the kubelet uses to talk to that runtime. As the CRI documentation describes, one part of it defines how container logs are handled: file names, directory locations, and line format. The CRI logging design proposal and the Kubernetes logging architecture page have the details.

Each container in a pod writes its logs to its own file, with everything the application sends to stdout and stderr (the standard streams). The files live on the node where the pod runs:

# pod container log file pattern
/var/log/pods/<namespace>_<podname>_<uid>/<container_name>/<restart-count>.log

# example
/var/log/pods/default_nginx-7f5c7d4f9b-abcde_12345/nginx-container/
  ├── 0.log   # first run of the container
  ├── 1.log   # run after the first restart
  └── ...

The file name is the container’s restart count. The first run writes 0.log. If the container crashes or restarts, the new run writes 1.log, then 2.log, and so on, while the previous file stays on disk. The kubelet keeps the logs of the most recent terminated run, which is what $ kubectl logs --previous <pod> -c <container> reads.

To make ingestion easier for third-party tools, the kubelet also creates a symbolic link to each container’s current log file in /var/log/containers/. The link name includes the pod name, namespace, container name, and container ID, so log shippers can identify each container:

# >>> symbolic link log file name pattern
/var/log/containers/<pod_name>_<namespace>_<container_name>-<container_id>.log

# >>> symbolic link log file name example
/var/log/containers/nginx-7f5c7d4f9b-abcde_default_nginx-container-12345.log

# >>> real file that the symbolic link points to
/var/log/pods/default_nginx-7f5c7d4f9b-abcde_12345/nginx-container/0.log

$ kubectl logs doesn’t use these links. They exist for log shippers such as Fluent Bit, Vector, and Filebeat. A link always points to the log file of the current run and doesn’t concatenate older runs. The container ID is part of the link name, so a restarted container gets a new link that points to its new log file. The same happens when the kubelet rotates a file: the path stays the same, but it’s a new file.

Log shippers must handle that. Fluent Bit, for example, tracks the inode of each file it reads. When a rotated file has the same name but a new inode, Fluent Bit treats it as a new file and reads it from the start. See the Tail input reference for the details.

The Kubernetes Log Line Format

The CRI defines the format of each line in the log file:

# >>> log line pattern
<timestamp> <stream> <flags> <message>

# >>> log line examples
2023-10-06T00:17:09.669794202Z stdout F Your log message here
2023-10-06T00:17:09.669794202Z stdout P Another log pt 1

  • timestamp: when the line was written, in RFC 3339 format with nanosecond precision.

  • stream: stdout or stderr.

  • flags: F for a full line, P for a partial line.

  • message: the raw log message from the container.

The P flag appears when a single line is longer than the runtime’s maximum log line size, 16 KiB by default in containerd (max_container_log_line_size). The runtime splits the line into chunks: each chunk except the last is written with P, and the last one with F. For example, an application that prints one 40 KB line produces three entries:

2025-06-21T22:15:10.123456789Z stdout P <first 16 KiB of the line>
2025-06-21T22:15:10.123456790Z stdout P <next 16 KiB of the line>
2025-06-21T22:15:10.123456791Z stdout F <rest of the line>

$ kubectl logs joins the partial chunks before showing them, so you see one line. Log shippers have to do the same. Fluent Bit, for example, does it with its built-in CRI multiline parser.

Managing Log Growth with Log Rotation

Logs can grow until they fill the node’s disk, which hurts observability in the cluster and the performance of the applications on that node. Even if an application logs very little, enforce size limits and rotation.

Log rotation for container logs is done by the kubelet. According to the log rotation documentation, the kubelet rotates each container log file when it reaches containerLogMaxSize (10Mi by default) and keeps at most containerLogMaxFiles files (5 by default). Configure these limits in the kubelet instead of using a third-party tool such as logrotate. Renaming, truncating, or closing files behind the kubelet’s back can corrupt its log management, and the log layout may change in future Kubernetes versions.

You set the limits in the kubelet configuration file:

/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml (excerpt)
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
containerLogMaxSize: 100Mi
containerLogMaxFiles: 5

Or with the equivalent kubelet flags, for example through the kubelet’s systemd unit:

/etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service
Environment="KUBELET_EXTRA_ARGS=--container-log-max-size=100Mi --container-log-max-files=5"

If you change the kubelet unit, put the change in a drop-in file instead of editing the unit itself, as I explain in Systemd Drop-in Overrides.

Shipping Kubernetes Logs to an External System

For search and long-term analysis, ship workload logs to a log analytics system such as OpenSearch, Elasticsearch, Grafana Loki, Splunk, or Datadog. Inside the cluster, tools such as Fluent Bit, Filebeat, and Vector read, process, and send the logs.

Whatever shipper you choose, the deployment pattern is the same. A DaemonSet is a Kubernetes workload that runs one pod on every node, and the DaemonSet for the shipper mounts the node’s /var/log directory with a hostPath volume. The shipper reads /var/log/containers/*.log, and because those links point into /var/log/pods/, the mount must include both directories. Mounting /var/log covers them. For example, a Fluent Bit DaemonSet:

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: fluent-bit
  namespace: default
  labels:
    app: fluent-bit
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: fluent-bit
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: fluent-bit
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: fluent-bit
      containers:
        - name: fluent-bit
          image: docker.io/bitnami/fluent-bit:4.0.3-debian-12-r0
          resources:
            limits:
              memory: "200Mi"
              cpu: "100m"
            requests:
              memory: "100Mi"
              cpu: "50m"
          volumeMounts: 
            - name: config
              mountPath: /opt/bitnami/fluent-bit/conf/fluent-bit.conf
              subPath: fluent-bit.conf
            # >>> MOUNTS THE NODE'S LOG DIRECTORY (BOTH /var/log/containers AND /var/log/pods)
            - name: varlog
              mountPath: /var/log
              readOnly: true
      volumes:
        - name: config
          configMap:
            name: fluent-bit-config
        # >>> ALLOWS THE FLUENT BIT POD TO READ THE LOG FILES OF PODS SCHEDULED ON THE NODE
        - name: varlog
          hostPath:
            path: /var/log
            type: Directory

Many log shippers can also add metadata such as pod labels and annotations to each log. For that, the shipper needs permission to read from the Kubernetes API, usually through a ClusterRole bound to its service account. This Fluent Bit ClusterRole is an example. I’ll cover metadata enrichment with Fluent Bit in a future post.

Once the logs are flowing, two problems usually come next. Fluent Bit can deliver a log more than once, which I address in Generating Log IDs with SHA-256 Hashes. And teams start counting log lines to build dashboards, which I argue against in Stop Extracting Metrics from OpenSearch Logs.

Key Takeaways

  • The container runtime writes each container’s stdout and stderr to /var/log/pods/<namespace>_<pod>_<uid>/<container>/<restart-count>.log on the node.

  • Each restart writes a new file. kubectl logs --previous reads the log of the previous run.

  • /var/log/containers/ holds symbolic links to the current log file of each container, for log shippers.

  • Each line follows the CRI format <timestamp> <stream> <flags> <message>. P marks a chunk of a line longer than the runtime’s limit, and F marks the end.

  • The kubelet rotates container logs with containerLogMaxSize and containerLogMaxFiles. Don’t use logrotate on these files.

  • Ship logs with a DaemonSet that mounts the node’s /var/log, not only /var/log/containers, because the links point into /var/log/pods.

References

  • Logging architecture (Kubernetes)

  • Container Runtime Interface (Kubernetes)

  • CRI logging design proposal (Kubernetes)

  • Kubelet configuration (Kubernetes)

  • DaemonSet (Kubernetes)

  • kubectl logs (Kubernetes)

  • Tail input (Fluent Bit)

  • containerd configuration (containerd)

  • Standard streams (Wikipedia)
