entry.title: Fluent Bit: Generating Log IDs with SHA-256 Hashes for Log Deduplication
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2025/06/19

This blog post explains why Fluent Bit can deliver the same log more than once, and why deduplication needs a unique ID derived from the log content. It then shows how to generate a SHA-256 hash of each log line with only native Fluent Bit features, without external scripts or plugins.

Why Fluent Bit Delivers Duplicate Logs

I ran into duplicated logs indexed in OpenSearch by Fluent Bit. After some research, I concluded that with the Tail input, Fluent Bit follows an at-least-once delivery strategy: a message is delivered one or more times, so duplicates can happen. It does not offer exactly-once delivery (each message delivered once) or at-most-once delivery (each message delivered once or not at all).

Several things contribute to this. For example, the Tail input can store its state in a database with DB On, and you can still get duplicates. The database only stores the read offset of each file, not whether each output received the record.

I plan to write a separate post about how Fluent Bit tracks delivery state (chunks, buffering, SQLite, storage type). For now, the important part is that duplicates can occur in situations such as an unavailable output or a Fluent Bit restart. That is expected behavior, not necessarily a bug, especially with several outputs configured.

Why You Need a Unique Log ID

With at-least-once delivery, a unique ID is a hard requirement to avoid duplicates at the destination. The ID must be derived from the log content, so the same line always gets the same ID. The destination can then overwrite the duplicate instead of storing a second copy.

If your stack has Logstash or OpenSearch ingest pipelines, the Logstash fingerprint filter and the OpenSearch fingerprint processor both hash selected fields for this. Fluent Bit has no filter dedicated to it. You could use a Lua or shell script callback, but that adds complexity and depends on external crypto libraries. The next section shows a workaround that uses only native Fluent Bit features.

If Fluent Bit sends logs directly to OpenSearch, the OpenSearch output has a Generate_ID On option. The ID it generates is not derived from the log line alone, so the same line read twice, for example after a restart, can get a different ID and still be stored twice. To deduplicate, generate the ID from the log content yourself.

Generating SHA-256 Hashes with Native Processors

I reviewed the Fluent Bit filters and found none that hash a field. Then I found the content modifier processor and its hash action. A processor is a step attached directly to an input or output in the YAML configuration. The hash action takes a record key and replaces its value with its SHA-256 hash. It’s meant for masking sensitive data such as passwords and PII, but it also works for building log IDs.

The key idea is to copy the log line to a new key and hash that copy. The original log line stays intact, and the hashed field becomes the log ID. For example:

/fluent-bit/fluent-bit.yaml
# The `pipeline.inputs.processors` feature is only available when using the `yaml` configuration format.  
# It is not supported in the legacy `.conf` configuration format.

pipeline:
  inputs:
    - name: dummy
      dummy: |
        {
          "message": "2025-06-19T17:02:35.123456789Z stdout F This is a Foobar application log sample running in kubernetes persisted on /var/log/containers/*.log"
        }
      tag: dummy.foobar
      processors:
        logs:
          # Copy the 'message' field to a new field called '_id'.
          - name: modify
            copy: message _id

          # Hash the '_id' field to anonymize or deduplicate.
          - name: content_modifier
            action: hash
            key: _id

    - name: dummy
      dummy: |
        {
          "message": "2025-06-19T17:02:35.123456789Z stdout F This is a Greeting application log sample running in kubernetes persisted on /var/log/containers/*.log"
        }
      tag: dummy.greeting 
      processors:
        logs:
          # Copy the 'message' field to a new field called '_id'.
          - name: modify
            copy: message _id

          # Hash the '_id' field to anonymize or deduplicate.
          - name: content_modifier
            action: hash
            key: _id

  outputs:
    - name: stdout
      format: json_lines
      match: "dummy.*"

The output looks like this. The same line always gets the same _id:

{
  "date": 1750366003.411804,
  "message": "2025-06-19T17:02:35.123456789Z stdout F This is a Foobar application log sample running in kubernetes persisted on /var/log/containers/*.log",
  "_id": "19a93f55808eb5478c65813c028045f1b354abe12790eb8aee0dd825697aa93e"
}
{
  "date": 1750366003.415653,
  "message": "2025-06-19T17:02:35.123456789Z stdout F This is a Greeting application log sample running in kubernetes persisted on /var/log/containers/*.log",
  "_id": "148917c2efe0114da7f7cef6327bde63f5c9ec5cac5cf05d4a73acefaa69a55c"
}
{
  "date": 1750366004.412541,
  "message": "2025-06-19T17:02:35.123456789Z stdout F This is a Foobar application log sample running in kubernetes persisted on /var/log/containers/*.log",
  "_id": "19a93f55808eb5478c65813c028045f1b354abe12790eb8aee0dd825697aa93e"
}
{
  "date": 1750366004.413101,
  "message": "2025-06-19T17:02:35.123456789Z stdout F This is a Greeting application log sample running in kubernetes persisted on /var/log/containers/*.log",
  "_id": "148917c2efe0114da7f7cef6327bde63f5c9ec5cac5cf05d4a73acefaa69a55c"
}

The hash action takes the bytes of the log line, applies SHA-256, and writes the result as a hexadecimal string. This Python snippet produces the same hash as Fluent Bit:

import hashlib

log_line_in_string = "2025-06-19T17:02:35.123456789Z stdout F This is a Foobar application log sample running in kubernetes persisted on /var/log/containers/*.log"

log_line_in_bytes = log_line_in_string.encode("utf-8")
log_line_in_sha256_hexa_decimal = hashlib.sha256(log_line_in_bytes).hexdigest()

print(log_line_in_sha256_hexa_decimal)
>>> "19a93f55808eb5478c65813c028045f1b354abe12790eb8aee0dd825697aa93e"

Using the Hash as the Document ID

Identical log lines always produce the same hash, so the destination can detect the duplicate. Because the raw container log line includes a nanosecond timestamp, two different events almost never share the same content.

To use the hash as the document ID in OpenSearch, point the OpenSearch output’s Id_Key option at the hashed field. A retried or re-read log then overwrites the existing document instead of creating a new one. OpenSearch treats _id as a metadata field and rejects it inside the document body, so in a real pipeline give the hashed field another name, such as log_id, and set Id_Key log_id.

Note

A complete, working example of this configuration is in my Docker Compose lab: github.com/c-neto/my-devops-labs/blog/2025-06-19

The Tail input in these examples reads the container log files that Kubernetes writes under /var/log/containers/. I explain how those files are created and rotated in Kubernetes Logs Simplified. Processors can also turn logs into metrics during ingestion, as I show in Stop Extracting Metrics from OpenSearch Logs.

Key Takeaways

  • With the Tail input, Fluent Bit delivers at least once, so duplicates are expected after output failures or restarts.

  • DB On stores file offsets, not per-output delivery status, so it doesn’t prevent duplicates.

  • Deduplication needs an ID derived from the log content. Generate_ID On isn’t derived from the log line alone.

  • Copy the log line to a new key with modify, then hash it with the content_modifier processor’s hash action to get a SHA-256 ID.

  • Processors on inputs are only available in the YAML configuration format.

  • Use the hashed field as the OpenSearch document ID with Id_Key, and don’t name it _id, because OpenSearch rejects that field in the document body.

References

  • Content modifier processor: hash (Fluent Bit)

  • Tail input (Fluent Bit)

  • OpenSearch output (Fluent Bit)

  • Fingerprint filter plugin (Logstash)

  • Fingerprint processor (OpenSearch)

  • Docker Compose lab for this post (GitHub)

entry.title: Helm Charts: Development Practices from a Programmer's Perspective
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2025/02/25

This blog post applies programming principles to Helm chart development. It covers when Helm’s complexity pays for itself, how it removes duplicated manifests (DRY), why over-templating hurts (YAGNI), and how library charts keep patterns reusable.

In the last quarter of 2024, I went deep into Helm charts and hit several challenges. At first, creating a new chart felt like added complexity, and I didn’t see a clear advantage over Kustomize. After days of reading about Helm, studying existing projects, and thinking it through, I started to see Helm as an ally instead of an overcomplicated tool. These are the main lessons.

Why Helm Charts Are a Good Tool for IaC

Helm is a package manager for Kubernetes, and a Helm chart is a package of templated Kubernetes manifests plus the default values that fill them. Helm renders the templates with Go templates, so a chart can abstract a workload behind a small set of parameters. That makes it a strong tool for Infrastructure as Code (IaC).

One of Helm’s main advantages is that charts are distributed as versioned artifacts, much like programming language packages or RPM and DEB packages. A chart can declare other charts as dependencies, so new solutions can be built on top of proven components.

Charts can be stored as OCI artifacts in registries such as AWS Elastic Container Registry (ECR), or as tarball files, which makes deployments reproducible. CD tools such as Spinnaker and Argo CD deploy Helm charts natively.

Helm is most useful for reusable infrastructure components deployed to several clusters with environment-specific configuration. It reduces duplicated manifests in Git and makes them easier to maintain.

Simple Made Easy: Is Helm Overengineering?

“Complexity has to pay for itself. It has to buy you something.”
Rich Hickey, Simple Made Easy (2011)

My first reaction to Helm was: “Oh my God, this is so complex. Am I just adding complexity?” Like any new tool, Helm has a learning curve. The way past it is to understand the problem Helm solves. If you think Helm is complex, try maintaining several nearly identical Kubernetes manifests that differ by a few parameters per cluster. That is a recipe for chaos.

Helm is overengineering only if it solves a problem you don’t have. Its complexity pays for itself when it removes a bigger problem, such as the same manifests duplicated across environments. When you manage workloads across several clusters, Helm isn’t overhead, it’s the trade-off that keeps them maintainable.

DRY: Removing Duplicated Kubernetes Manifests

“DRY (Don’t Repeat Yourself) is about the duplication of knowledge, of intent. It’s about expressing the same thing in two different places, possibly in two totally different ways.”
Andrew Hunt and David Thomas, The Pragmatic Programmer

Most companies keep separate environments for each stage of development: a development environment for internal testing, a staging environment for validation, and a production environment for real users.

In that setup, you usually run the same applications on several Kubernetes clusters with small differences, such as Ingress settings, resource requests, and environment variables. The simplest approach is one set of manifests per environment, with the same structure and different values. It works, but it creates duplicated code.

Duplicated manifests increase the risk of errors and drift. With one or two environments, it’s manageable. With three or more, it stops scaling: a single fix has to be applied to several files.

Helm avoids that with templates. The structure of the manifests lives in the chart, and each environment has its own values file with only the parameters that change. For example:

templates/deployment.yaml (excerpt)
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          resources:
            {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }}
values-dev.yaml
replicaCount: 1
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 100m
values-prod.yaml
replicaCount: 3
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "1"

$ helm upgrade --install my-app ./my-app -f values-prod.yaml

One chart renders the manifests for every environment from its values file. That keeps environments consistent, makes fixes a one-place change, and reduces errors.

YAGNI: Avoid Over-Templating

“Always implement things when you actually need them, never when you just foresee that you need them.”
Ron Jeffries, on the XP principle “You aren’t gonna need it” (YAGNI)

YAGNI (You Aren’t Gonna Need It) is the principle that you should not build features or abstractions before you actually need them. In Helm, it means creating templates only for structures that are well defined and actually repeated. A common mistake is over-templating: so many parameters that the chart is flexible on paper but hard to maintain.

If you’re writing many template functions to handle every possible variation in values.yaml, the template probably lacks a clear structure. Instead of simplifying deployments, it adds complexity that makes debugging and maintenance harder.

Worse than having no template is maintaining template functions that are never used. Every extra function, conditional, or parameter adds cognitive load. A team that inherits a chart full of unused logic has to understand and maintain complexity that adds nothing. Solve the problems you have now, not hypothetical future ones.

Library Charts: Reusable Patterns

Helm has two chart types: application and library. An application chart is a complete package that you deploy, with all the Kubernetes resources an application needs. A library chart holds reusable templates and functions that other charts use, and it is never deployed on its own. It works as an abstraction layer for components that many charts share.

A good example is the Bitnami Common library chart. Its functions and patterns are used across the whole Bitnami charts repository, which keeps their charts consistent and easier to maintain:

  • Bitnami Common library chart

  • How the Bitnami Fluent Bit chart uses it

Helm as a Way to Think About Infrastructure

Programming principles such as DRY, YAGNI, and modular design make Helm charts much better. Helm is more than a templating tool for Kubernetes manifests: it’s a way to think about infrastructure as modular, reusable components, something any developer can appreciate. Applied with care, these practices let teams scale their deployments with less overhead and keep them easy to maintain.

When a chart grows, debugging what the templates receive becomes the hard part. I wrote about a trick for that in Helm Tips: Inspect Your Chart Context with JSON. I also use Helm to template Logstash pipelines, as I describe in Logstash DB Enrichment.

Key Takeaways

  • Helm renders Kubernetes manifests from Go templates and values, and distributes charts as versioned packages, including OCI artifacts.

  • Helm’s complexity pays for itself when it removes a bigger problem, such as near-identical manifests across several clusters.

  • Keep one chart and one values file per environment instead of one copy of every manifest per environment.

  • Don’t over-template. Parameterize only what really changes, and remove functions and options nobody uses.

  • Use library charts, such as Bitnami Common, to share templates and functions across charts.

References

  • Chart best practices (Helm)

  • Library charts (Helm)

  • Yagni (Martin Fowler)

  • Don’t repeat yourself (Wikipedia)

  • Anti-pattern (Wikipedia)

  • The Twelve-Factor App (12factor.net)

  • Bitnami Common library chart (GitHub)

I’m Carlos Neto, and this blog is where I share my experiences and open source contributions. More about me on my home page. If you have questions or a different approach, contact me on LinkedIn.

entry.title: Logstash DB Enrichment: Tips and Traps
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2025/02/16

This blog post covers the lessons from enriching logs in Logstash with data from a PostgreSQL database. It explains hidden behaviors of the jdbc_streaming filter that can stop log ingestion, and the JDBC connection string parameters that prevent them. These problems are hard to reproduce and not clearly documented, so I hope these tips save you hours of troubleshooting and forum searching.

The examples assume Logstash OSS 8.17.2 running in Kubernetes with a PostgreSQL database, but the same considerations apply to a single instance or another relational database. I also built a Docker Compose lab where you can try every tip in this post: github.com/c-neto/my-devops-labs/logstash/db-enrichment

Special thanks to PostgreSQL specialist Lucio Chiessi for helping me explore the JDBC connection string options that are useful for Logstash.

Use Prepared Statements

The first tip is to enable use_prepared_statements in the jdbc_streaming filter.

A prepared statement is a SQL query that PostgreSQL parses and plans once, then runs many times with different parameters. It’s faster, because the plan is not rebuilt on every call, and safer, because parameters are bound instead of concatenated, which prevents SQL injection. An enrichment query is a perfect fit: its structure never changes, only the parameter does, and it runs for every log. For example:

jdbc_streaming {
  jdbc_driver_library => "/usr/share/logstash/postgresql.jar"
  jdbc_driver_class => "org.postgresql.Driver"
  jdbc_connection_string => "${DB_JDBC_CONNECTION_STRING}"
  jdbc_user => "${DB_USER}"
  jdbc_password => "${DB_PASSWORD}"
  use_prepared_statements => true
  prepared_statement_name => "logstash_enrich_query"
  prepared_statement_bind_values => [
    "[document][user_id]"
  ]
  statement => "
  SELECT
    user_name,
    user_email,
    user_group
  FROM table_users
  WHERE id = ?
  "
  target => "sql"
}

When the Database Is Down, Your Pipeline Won’t Start

When a pipeline uses jdbc_streaming, Logstash checks the database connection before the pipeline starts receiving logs. If the database is down, the pipeline is not registered and receives nothing. The check happens at startup, not when a log reaches the filter. So even if none of your logs match the if condition that leads to the enrichment, the whole pipeline stays down.

There is a detail that makes this confusing. If the database is up when the pipeline starts and the connection breaks later, the pipeline keeps running and only the enrichment fails. When the connection comes back, enrichment works again.

The consequence is that enrichment creates a hard dependency between every new Logstash instance and the database. If the database is down, new Logstash pods can’t start their pipelines, so scaling doesn’t help, and a simple restart blocks ingestion.

I didn’t find any parameter in the Logstash documentation to change this. One workaround is to split the logs into two pipelines: one for logs that always need enrichment and one for logs that never do, so a database outage only affects the first. That can duplicate code, so my suggestion is to generate the pipeline from a template, with a fallback version that leaves out the jdbc_streaming block. On Kubernetes, I template the pipeline with Helm (see Helm Charts: Development Practices). Outside Kubernetes, Jinja works well. Logstash Modular Pipelines shows another way to compose pipelines without repeating inputs and outputs.

Table Lock = Frozen Log Ingestion

This is the worst one: logs stop flowing and nothing explicitly tells you why.

If a log reaches jdbc_streaming while the queried table is locked, the query waits, and the whole pipeline stops behind it, including logs that don’t use the enrichment. At the default log level, Logstash doesn’t log anything that points to the lock.

The jdbc_streaming documentation has no parameter for this, so I looked at the PostgreSQL JDBC driver instead. That explained the behavior: by default, a query waiting for a locked table waits forever.

The fix is to add options=-c lock_timeout=1000 to the JDBC connection string. lock_timeout is the maximum time, in milliseconds, that a statement waits to acquire a lock. With 1000, if the lock isn’t acquired within 1 second, the query fails, Logstash logs an explicit lock timeout error, the log continues through the pipeline without the enrichment, and the next logs keep flowing.

To reproduce it, lock the table in PostgreSQL:

LOCK TABLE table_used_by_logstash IN ACCESS EXCLUSIVE MODE;

After that, I reviewed every JDBC connection parameter that defaults to infinite and could cause a similar freeze. The next sections cover them.

Slow Query = Slow Log Ingestion

The query execution timeout also defaults to infinite in PostgreSQL. If the database is overloaded or throttled and an enrichment query takes a long time, every log in the pipeline queues behind it, just like with a lock.

Set options=-c statement_timeout=5000 in the JDBC connection string. statement_timeout is the maximum time, in milliseconds, that a query can run before PostgreSQL cancels it. With 5000, queries longer than 5 seconds are aborted, the error appears in the Logstash logs, enrichment is skipped and the failure tag is added to the event, and the pipeline keeps working.

To simulate a slow query, add pg_sleep to the statement. In this example, pg_sleep(10)::text makes every query take 10 seconds:

jdbc_streaming {
  jdbc_driver_library => "/usr/share/logstash/postgresql.jar"
  jdbc_driver_class => "org.postgresql.Driver"
  jdbc_connection_string => "${DB_JDBC_CONNECTION_STRING}"
  jdbc_user => "${DB_USER}"
  jdbc_password => "${DB_PASSWORD}"
  use_prepared_statements => true
  prepared_statement_name => "logstash_enrich_query"
  prepared_statement_bind_values => ["[document][user_id]"]
  statement => "
    SELECT
      pg_sleep(10)::text,    
      user_name,
      user_email,
      user_group
    FROM table_users
    WHERE id = ?
  "
  target => "sql"
}

Set Login and Socket Timeouts

For the same reason, set two more connection parameters:

  • loginTimeout=10: the maximum time, in seconds, to wait for a connection to be established. After that, the driver throws an error.

  • socketTimeout=10: the maximum time, in seconds, to wait for data from the database on a socket read. After that, the connection is closed.

Identify Logstash Connections in the Database

Enrichment queries can put real load on the database, so the database team needs to see which connections come from Logstash. Set ApplicationName=logstash in the connection string, and every Logstash connection shows up under that name. For example, this query lists them:

SELECT pid, application_name, usename, datname, client_addr, state
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE application_name = 'logstash';

Putting all the parameters from this post together, a connection string looks like this (spaces inside options are URL-encoded as %20):

jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/db?ApplicationName=logstash&loginTimeout=10&socketTimeout=10&options=-c%20lock_timeout=1000%20-c%20statement_timeout=5000

Sequel Options Are Not Database Connection Parameters

Don’t mix up sequel_opts and the JDBC connection string. They play different roles. Logstash talks to the database through JDBC, but it manages the connections with the Sequel library in JRuby, which sequel_opts configures. The JDBC connection string defines how the database behaves for the session. Sequel defines how Logstash manages its pool of connections.

For example, sequel_opts::pool_timeout is how long Logstash waits for a free connection in its pool. It has nothing to do with how long a query may run, which is a database setting defined in jdbc_connection_string:

jdbc_streaming {
  sequel_opts => {
    max_connections => 4
    pool_timeout => 5
  }
  jdbc_connection_string => "jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/db?options=-c%20statement_timeout=1000%20"
}

Test Before You Trust the Defaults

When I started with Logstash, I assumed its behavior was simple and that the defaults were safe. They aren’t always. Logstash has many details that can slow down log ingestion or stop it completely.

As requirements grow, so do the surprises. Don’t take anything for granted, and test it. I highly recommend a Docker Compose lab to try features in different situations before production. It makes the setup more reliable, helps you plan workarounds, and avoids nasty surprises, especially late on a Friday night.

Don’t forget to check out the lab: github.com/c-neto/my-devops-labs/logstash/db-enrichment

Key Takeaways

  • Enable use_prepared_statements in jdbc_streaming: enrichment queries have a fixed structure and run for every log.

  • A pipeline with jdbc_streaming doesn’t start if the database is down at startup, even for logs that never reach the enrichment. Keep a fallback pipeline without it.

  • PostgreSQL waits forever for a locked table by default. Set lock_timeout so a lock can’t freeze ingestion.

  • Query execution has no timeout by default either. Set statement_timeout so a slow database can’t queue every log.

  • Set loginTimeout and socketTimeout, and ApplicationName=logstash so the database team can identify Logstash connections.

  • sequel_opts controls Logstash’s connection pool. The JDBC connection string controls the database session. They are not interchangeable.

References

  • jdbc_streaming filter plugin (Logstash)

  • Client connection defaults: lock_timeout and statement_timeout (PostgreSQL)

  • Connection parameters (PostgreSQL JDBC driver)

  • Opening databases: PostgreSQL options (Sequel)

entry.title: OpenSearch Concepts: Index and Shards
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2025/01/05

This blog post explains two of the most basic concepts in OpenSearch administration: indices and shards. It covers what primary and replica shards are, how their counts affect performance and fault tolerance, and the API calls I use most to inspect indices and shards while troubleshooting.

Understanding Indices and Shards

An index is a logical namespace for a collection of documents and their characteristics, such as field types, lifecycle policies, and storage tier. OpenSearch stores those documents on disk in partitions called shards.

A shard is one partition of an index, and each shard is a full Lucene index. As the OpenSearch introduction describes, shards come in two kinds:

  • Primary shards receive every write and can also serve reads.

  • Replica shards are copies of the primaries. They provide fault tolerance and serve reads, which spreads the query load.

An index can have one or more shards spread across several nodes. That distribution is what lets an OpenSearch cluster scale an index beyond one machine and survive the loss of a node.

Primary shards

Replica shards

Purpose

Hold the data and receive every write

Copies of the primaries for fault tolerance and reads

More of them means

More parallel indexing, until shards get too small

More read capacity and more copies to survive node failures

Can change after creation?

Only with split, shrink, or reindex

Yes, at any time

More primary shards spread writes across more partitions and nodes, which raises indexing throughput. More replicas add fault tolerance and more nodes that can answer queries.

The number of primary shards is set when the index is created. Changing it later means creating a new index with the split or shrink APIs, or reindexing. Choose it carefully, based on your query load and, above all, your write load. Replicas can be changed at any time.

More shards are not always better, though. Every shard costs heap, file handles, and cluster state, so many small shards hurt more than they help. I wrote about one way to avoid that in Avoiding Over-Sharding in OpenSearch with Filtered Aliases.

Note

A primary shard and its replica are never allocated to the same node. If that node fails, the other copy is still available.

Useful API Calls for Indices and Shards

These calls help with troubleshooting and monitoring indices and shards. You can run them in OpenSearch Dashboards » Dev Tools or with an HTTP client such as cURL or Postman.

  • List all indices, sorted by name (CAT indices):

GET _cat/indices?v&s=index

  • List the shards of a specific index:

GET <INDEX-NAME>/_search_shards

  • Get the index settings, for example the number of shards, replicas, and creation time:

GET <INDEX-NAME>/_settings

  • Get the field types defined in the index mapping:

GET <INDEX-NAME>/_mapping

  • Show the ISM policy attached to an index (ISM explain API):

GET _plugins/ism/explain/<INDEX-NAME>?show_policy=true

  • List shards that are not allocated to any node (status UNASSIGNED) and why (CAT shards):

GET _cat/shards?v&h=index,shard,prirep,state,unassigned.reason&s=state

  • Check how shards and disk are distributed across nodes (CAT allocation):

GET _cat/allocation?v

  • Follow shard recovery or relocation progress (CAT recovery):

GET _cat/recovery/<INDEX-NAME>?v&s=stage:desc

  • List all shards, sorted by index:

GET _cat/shards?v&s=index

  • List indices, sorted by size:

GET _cat/indices?v&h=index,store.size&s=store.size:desc

These calls answer most of my day-to-day questions about a cluster. When the allocation output shows nodes with very different disk usage, OpenSearch Shard Allocation: Balanced by Count, Rebalanced by Watermarks explains why. When you need to remove nodes, Scaling Down and Resizing OpenSearch Data Nodes shows how to move their shards safely first.

Key Takeaways

  • An index is a logical collection of documents. Shards are the partitions that store it, and each shard is a Lucene index.

  • Primary shards receive every write. Replica shards are copies that add fault tolerance and serve reads.

  • The number of primary shards is fixed at creation. Changing it requires split, shrink, or reindex. Replicas can change at any time.

  • More primaries raise write throughput, but too many small shards waste heap and cluster state.

  • A primary and its replica are never placed on the same node.

  • _cat/indices, _cat/shards, _cat/allocation, and _cat/recovery cover most troubleshooting questions about indices and shards.

  • Shrink index (OpenSearch)

  • CAT indices (OpenSearch)

  • CAT shards (OpenSearch)

  • CAT allocation (OpenSearch)

entry.title: Dynaconf: The Python Config Silver Bullet!
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2024/07/21

This blog post gives a short overview of good practices for application configuration, explains the main features of Dynaconf, and walks through a hands-on example that extends it to read parameters from AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store.

Twelve-Factor App: Good Practices for Application Config

Before talking about Dynaconf or any code, it helps to know the practices behind portable configuration.

The Twelve-Factor App is a methodology with a set of good practices for building modern applications that run anywhere, such as on SaaS platforms or Kubernetes clusters. It has a chapter dedicated to configuration, which defines what counts as configuration (anything that changes between deploys, such as credentials and resource addresses) and insists on keeping it strictly separate from code.

Python Config Libraries

Like most common needs with well-known practices, configuration has libraries to help. I have used a few good ones in Python:

  • python-dotenv reads simple key-value pairs from a .env file and can export them as environment variables.

  • python-decouple gives you one settings interface so you can change parameters without redeploying the app, which is useful for web applications.

  • Structured file parsers can also serve as config readers, such as PyYAML, json, tomllib, shlex, and configparser.

These modules have their use cases, especially for simple scripts where the standard library is enough. But, as the provocative title suggests, this post is about Dynaconf.

Dynaconf

Dynaconf is a configuration management library for Python, designed around the Twelve-Factor config principles. It sits between your code and your settings and gives you one interface to read parameters and secrets from files or external systems.

Its main features are:

  • Multiple config files in several formats (toml, yaml, json, ini), merged into one settings object.

  • Parameters from environment variables, which take precedence over files.

  • Layered environments (profiles) such as default, development, production.

  • A CLI that helps with debugging.

The feature I like most is reading parameters from external parameter and secret stores. Dynaconf has built-in support for HashiCorp Vault and Redis, and you can write your own loader for any other source. The example below does exactly that for AWS Parameter Store.

Talk Is Cheap, Show Me the Code!

This step-by-step guide sets up Dynaconf from scratch with two settings files, then adds a custom loader for the AWS Parameter Store service. LocalStack simulates AWS in a Docker container, so you don’t need an AWS account.

Note

All code is in this GitHub repository: github.com/c-neto/my-code-playground/blog-code-examples/2024-07-21-dynaconf-loaders

Step-by-step

  1. Create a virtual environment and install dependencies:

python3 -m venv venv
venv/bin/pip install dynaconf boto3 
source venv/bin/activate

  1. Use the Dynaconf CLI to create the settings files and config.py:

dynaconf init \
    -v PARAMETER_FROM_SETTINGS_TOML_FILE="foobar from settings.toml" \
    -s PARAMETER_FROM_SECRETS_TOML_FILE="foobar from .secrets.toml"

# » output
#
# ├── config.py       » python module with dynaconf instance
# ├── .secrets.toml   » settings files with: PARAMETER_FROM_SECRETS_TOML_FILE
# └── settings.toml   » settings files with: PARAMETER_FROM_SETTINGS_TOML_FILE

The config.py that the CLI creates looks like this:

config.py
from dynaconf import Dynaconf

settings = Dynaconf(
    envvar_prefix="DYNACONF",
    settings_files=['settings.toml', '.secrets.toml'],
)

The CLI can list the parameters that config.py loads:

dynaconf -i config.settings list 

# » output
#
# PARAMETER_FROM_SETTINGS_TOML_FILE<str> 'foobar from settings.toml'
# PARAMETER_FROM_SECRETS_TOML_FILE<str> 'foobar from .secrets.toml'

  1. Run LocalStack in a container to simulate the AWS Parameter Store service:

docker run --rm -it --detach \
    --name localstack \
    -p 4566:4566 \
    -e SERVICES=ssm,sts \
    -e DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1 \
    -e AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=test \
    -e AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=test \
    localstack/localstack:latest

  1. With LocalStack running, export the AWS environment variables that point to its API:

export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=test
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=test
export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=http://localhost:4566
export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1

  1. Create two parameters under the /my-application/ prefix, named PARAMETER_FROM_AWS_PARAMETER_STORE_1 and PARAMETER_FROM_AWS_PARAMETER_STORE_2:

aws ssm put-parameter \
    --name "/my-application/PARAMETER_FROM_AWS_PARAMETER_STORE_1" \
    --value "foo" \
    --type "SecureString" \
    --endpoint-url http://localhost:4566

aws ssm put-parameter \
    --name "/my-application/PARAMETER_FROM_AWS_PARAMETER_STORE_2" \
    --value "bar" \
    --type "SecureString" \
    --endpoint-url http://localhost:4566

  1. Edit config.py to add a custom loader that reads every parameter under /my-application/ from AWS Parameter Store. A Dynaconf loader is a module with a load() function that Dynaconf calls to add values to the settings. If there is no AWS session, the code falls back to the environment loader only:

config.py
import logging

import boto3
from botocore.exceptions import ClientError, BotoCoreError
from dynaconf import Dynaconf, LazySettings
from dynaconf.loaders.base import SourceMetadata

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
PARAMETERS_PREFIX = "/my-application/"


# Retrieve parameters from AWS Parameter Store recursively by prefix
def _aws_parameter_store_loader(parameters_prefix: str) -> dict:
    ssm_client = boto3.client('ssm')

    paginator = ssm_client.get_paginator("get_parameters_by_path")
    pages = paginator.paginate(Path=parameters_prefix, Recursive=True, WithDecryption=True)

    parameters_from_aws_raw = {}

    for page in pages:
        for param in page["Parameters"]:
            name_full = param["Name"]
            value = param["Value"]
            parameters_from_aws_raw[name_full] = value

    parameters_from_aws = {}

    for name_full, value in parameters_from_aws_raw.items():
        try:
            *_, name = name_full.split("/")
        except ValueError:
            logger.warning(f'Parameter name pattern outside of expected format, skipping: "{name_full}"')
        else:
            parameters_from_aws[name] = value

    return parameters_from_aws


# Dynaconf callback - used in this case for retrieve parameters from AWS Parameter Store
def load(obj: LazySettings, env: str, silent: bool = True, key: str = None, filename: str = None) -> None:
    global parameters_from_aws

    source_metadata = SourceMetadata('aws-parameter-store', PARAMETERS_PREFIX)
    obj.update(parameters_from_aws, loader_identifier=source_metadata)
    logger.debug(f"Parameters loaded from AWS Parameter Store: {list(parameters_from_aws)}")


# Attempt to load parameters from AWS Parameter Store and update Dynaconf loaders
try:
    parameters_from_aws = _aws_parameter_store_loader(PARAMETERS_PREFIX)
except (BotoCoreError, ClientError) as e:
    LOADERS_FOR_DYNACONF = ["dynaconf.loaders.env_loader"]
    logger.warning("AWS active session not detected, skipping load parameters from AWS Parameter Store")
else:
    # __name__ is module name that have "load()" callback. It could be another module...
    LOADERS_FOR_DYNACONF = [__name__, "dynaconf.loaders.env_loader"]


# Initialize Dynaconf settings with specified files and loaders
settings = Dynaconf(
    settings_files=["settings.toml", ".secrets.toml"],
    envvar_prefix="MY_APP",
    LOADERS_FOR_DYNACONF=LOADERS_FOR_DYNACONF,
)

  1. List the settings again. PARAMETER_FROM_AWS_PARAMETER_STORE_1 and PARAMETER_FROM_AWS_PARAMETER_STORE_2 now come from AWS Parameter Store:

dynaconf -i config.settings list

# » output
#
# PARAMETER_FROM_SETTINGS_TOML_FILE<str> 'foobar from settings.toml'
# PARAMETER_FROM_SECRETS_TOML_FILE<str> 'foobar from .secrets.toml'
# PARAMETER_FROM_AWS_PARAMETER_STORE_1<str> 'foo'
# PARAMETER_FROM_AWS_PARAMETER_STORE_2<str> 'bar'

  1. Environment variables take precedence over every other source. To see it, export MY_APP_PARAMETER_FROM_AWS_PARAMETER_STORE_2:

export MY_APP_PARAMETER_FROM_AWS_PARAMETER_STORE_2="param from environment variable"

Dynaconf only reads environment variables that start with the envvar_prefix value, MY_APP in this case.

Now PARAMETER_FROM_AWS_PARAMETER_STORE_2 returns the value from the environment variable:

dynaconf -i config.settings list

# » output
# 
# PARAMETER_FROM_SETTINGS_TOML_FILE<str> 'foobar from settings.toml'
# PARAMETER_FROM_SECRETS_TOML_FILE<str> 'foobar from .secrets.toml'
# PARAMETER_FROM_AWS_PARAMETER_STORE_1<str> 'foo'
# PARAMETER_FROM_AWS_PARAMETER_STORE_2<str> 'param from environment variable'

The inspect command shows where each value came from:

dynaconf -i config.settings inspect

# » output
# 
# {
#   "header": {
#     "env_filter": "None",
#     "key_filter": "None",
#     "new_first": "True",
#     "history_limit": "None",
#     "include_internal": "False"
#   },
#   "current": {
#     "PARAMETER_FROM_SETTINGS_TOML_FILE": "foobar from settings.toml",
#     "PARAMETER_FROM_SECRETS_TOML_FILE": "foobar from .secrets.toml",
#     "PARAMETER_FROM_AWS_PARAMETER_STORE_1": "foo",
#     "PARAMETER_FROM_AWS_PARAMETER_STORE_2": "bar"
#   },
#   "history": [
#     {
#       "loader": "aws-parameter-store",
#       "identifier": "/my-application/",
#       "env": "global",
#       "merged": false,
#       "value": {
#         "PARAMETER_FROM_AWS_PARAMETER_STORE_1": "foo",
#         "PARAMETER_FROM_AWS_PARAMETER_STORE_2": "bar"
#       }
#     },
#     {
#       "loader": "toml",
#       "identifier": ".secrets.toml",
#       "env": "default",
#       "merged": false,
#       "value": {
#         "PARAMETER_FROM_SECRETS_TOML_FILE": "foobar from .secrets.toml"
#       }
#     },
#     {
#       "loader": "toml",
#       "identifier": "settings.toml",
#       "env": "default",
#       "merged": false,
#       "value": {
#         "PARAMETER_FROM_SETTINGS_TOML_FILE": "foobar from settings.toml"
#       }
#     },
#     {
#       "loader": "set_method",
#       "identifier": "settings_module_method",
#       "env": "global",
#       "merged": false,
#       "value": {
#         "SETTINGS_MODULE": [
#           "settings.toml",
#           ".secrets.toml"
#         ]
#       }
#     },
#     {
#       "loader": "set_method",
#       "identifier": "init_kwargs",
#       "env": "global",
#       "merged": false,
#       "value": {
#         "LOADERS_FOR_DYNACONF": [
#           "config",
#           "dynaconf.loaders.env_loader"
#         ],
#         "SETTINGS_FILE_FOR_DYNACONF": [
#           "settings.toml",
#           ".secrets.toml"
#         ],
#         "ENVVAR_PREFIX_FOR_DYNACONF": "MY_APP"
#       }
#     }
#   ]
# }

Why I Use Dynaconf

I have been using Dynaconf for about 4 years, and I like how it solves common configuration problems in a simple, direct way. Before, I used PyYAML, but I kept writing the same code to read configuration and secrets from different files. When a mix of sources was needed, such as YAML and environment variables, the code grew more complex and pulled attention away from the problem the system was supposed to solve.

The first time I tried Dynaconf, its ability to merge several config files, including nested parameters, impressed me. It’s especially useful for keeping sensitive values in their own file.

Today, I only skip Dynaconf when a project requires the standard library only. Otherwise, I don’t see a reason not to use it, especially in applications that run on Kubernetes. I really like the module and suggest you give it a try!

If you write Python for operations work, two other posts may interest you: groupby + attrgetter for grouping objects without loops, and OpenTelemetry for instrumenting a Python application.

Key Takeaways

  • The Twelve-Factor App says configuration is anything that changes between deploys, and it must live outside the code.

  • python-dotenv, python-decouple, and file parsers such as PyYAML cover simple cases, but mixing sources with them means writing glue code.

  • Dynaconf merges several config files and formats, environment variables, and environment profiles into one settings object.

  • Environment variables with the configured prefix (MY_APP_ in the example) override every other source.

  • A custom loader is a module with a load() function, added to LOADERS_FOR_DYNACONF. The example reads every parameter under /my-application/ from AWS Parameter Store.

  • dynaconf list and dynaconf inspect show the final values and which loader set each one.

References

entry.title: Logstash Sniffing: Improving Log Ingestion in OpenSearch Scalable Clusters
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2024/06/08

This blog post covers a common problem when Logstash ships logs to an OpenSearch cluster with autoscaling ingest nodes behind a load balancer: one node takes all the traffic while the others sit idle. It shows how the output plugin’s sniffing options fix that by discovering the nodes from the OpenSearch API.

The Problem: One Ingest Node Takes All the Traffic

An ingest node is an OpenSearch node that preprocesses documents before they are indexed. The node types documentation describes how a cluster can have dedicated ingest nodes, and on Kubernetes they are often scaled with a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) and reached through a load balancer.

That setup has a catch when Logstash is the shipper. Shipping logs over HTTP is stateless, but Logstash keeps a persistent connection to the node the load balancer picked first. As long as that connection stays open, every log goes to the same node. That node gets overloaded while the other ingest nodes are underused. If the HPA scales on average resource usage, the imbalance also hides the real load, so the autoscaler reacts too late or not at all.

The Solution: Let Logstash Discover the Nodes

The hosts parameter of the output plugin accepts one address or several. With several addresses, Logstash balances the traffic across them. For a fixed set of ingest nodes, listing them all solves the problem. For nodes that scale up and down, a static list goes stale quickly.

Sniffing is the output plugin’s answer for dynamic clusters: Logstash periodically asks the cluster which nodes exist and updates its host list. The sniffing parameters read the node addresses from the Nodes Info API. The OpenSearch output plugin is a fork of the Elasticsearch one and keeps these options. For example:

output {
  opensearch {
    hosts           => "https://opensearch-load-balancer:9200"
    sniffing        => true
    sniffing_delay  => 30
    sniffing_path   => "/_nodes/ingest:true"
    ...
  }
}

When Logstash starts, it calls /_nodes/ingest:true to get the addresses of all ingest nodes, and adds them to its host list. Every 30 seconds, it calls the API again, adding new nodes and removing the ones that are gone. The load balancer address is only used to reach that API.

The sniffing_path parameter selects which nodes to use. For example, /_nodes/data:true sends logs straight to the data nodes.

Two things are worth checking before you enable it. Logstash connects to the addresses the nodes publish, so they must be reachable from where Logstash runs. If Logstash runs outside the Kubernetes cluster, pod IPs usually aren’t. And if the connection uses TLS, the node certificates must be valid for those addresses, not only for the load balancer’s hostname.

Why I Use Sniffing

With sniffing enabled, the traffic spreads evenly across the ingest nodes. It also takes the load balancer out of the data path, removes an extra network hop, and makes better use of resources. The HPA also gets a realistic view of the load, so scaling works the way it should.

It’s simple and effective enough that I miss it in other log shippers, such as Fluent Bit. I have been using this approach, and the results are really nice!

For more on how OpenSearch places the data once it arrives, see OpenSearch Concepts: Index and Shards. If your Logstash configuration is growing across many applications, Logstash Modular Pipelines shows how I keep it organized.

Key Takeaways

  • Behind a load balancer, Logstash keeps a persistent connection to one OpenSearch node and sends all logs to it.

  • That overloads one ingest node, leaves the others idle, and gives the autoscaler a misleading average.

  • A static list in hosts works for a fixed set of nodes, but not for nodes that scale up and down.

  • sniffing => true with sniffing_path => "/_nodes/ingest:true" makes Logstash discover the ingest nodes and refresh the list every sniffing_delay seconds.

  • The load balancer address is only used to reach the Nodes Info API.

  • The published node addresses must be reachable from Logstash, and TLS certificates must cover them.

References

  • Elasticsearch output plugin: sniffing options (Logstash)

  • logstash-output-opensearch (GitHub)

  • Creating a cluster: node types (OpenSearch)

  • Nodes Info API (OpenSearch)

entry.title: fzf: Life is Too Short for Pipe Grep
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2024/04/28

This blog post explains why fzf, a command-line fuzzy finder, replaced Ctrl + R, find, and command | grep in my terminal. It also shows how to configure its Zsh widgets for searching history, files, and directories, with live previews.

Searching in the Terminal Is Tedious

Searching in the terminal is something you do all the time, and it gets boring fast. Three cases show the problem: searching command history, searching files and directories, and searching command output.

To recall a command, most people press the up and down arrows. Most shells also have an interactive search on Ctrl + R. In Zsh it’s reverse-i-search. It works, but you have to press the shortcut again to see each older match, which is painful when you ran the same command many times with different arguments.

To find a file or directory, the usual tool is $ find. It works well when you know exactly what you’re looking for, but not when you only remember part of the path.

To find something in a command’s output, the usual method is $ command | grep. It has the same problem as find: depending on the case, you run grep several times until you find what you need.

That routine pushed me to look for a better way to search interactively.

Fuzzy Finders Are the Solution

After a few days of research, I found fzf, a cross-platform fuzzy finder written in Go.

A fuzzy finder is a search tool that finds files, directories, or any other items even when you don’t remember their exact names. It uses fuzzy matching, so partial words, characters out of order, and typos still find the right result.

fzf filters a list as you type, so you don’t need $ command | grep anymore. It reads the output of any command for interactive searching. For example, $ kgp -A | fzf searches pods across a Kubernetes cluster (kgp is the kubectl get pods alias from the kubectl plugin I use in Zsh). fzf also ships shell widgets that search files, directories, and command history.

fzf has widgets for Fish, Bash, and Zsh. You can see them in github.com/junegunn/fzf/shell.

How to Configure fzf Widgets in Zsh

First, install fzf. The installation section lists several options. Package managers can ship an old version, so I download the latest release from GitHub:

setopt INTERACTIVE_COMMENTS

# download the release (at the publish date of this post, the latest version was 0.50.0)
curl -L https://github.com/junegunn/fzf/releases/download/0.50.0/fzf-0.50.0-linux_amd64.tar.gz > fzf-0.50.0-linux_amd64.tar.gz

# uncompress the downloaded file to access the fzf binary
tar -xzvf fzf-0.50.0-linux_amd64.tar.gz

# check fzf binary execution
./fzf --help

# move the binary to a folder present in your path
mv fzf /usr/local/bin/

By default, fzf uses $ find to list files and directories. You can change that. I use fd, a faster and friendlier alternative to find:

# In Linux workstation with dnf package manager
dnf install fd-find

# In MacOs workstation with homebrew package manager
brew install fd

For file previews, I use bat, a cat clone with syntax highlighting:

# In Linux workstation with dnf package manager
dnf install bat

# In MacOs workstation with homebrew package manager
brew install bat

For directory previews, I use tree, which prints the contents of a directory recursively as a tree:

# In Linux workstation with dnf package manager
dnf install tree

# In MacOs workstation with homebrew package manager
brew install tree

Now load the widgets. Since version 0.48.0, fzf prints the setup code for a shell when you pass its name (--zsh, --fish, or --bash):

# Set up fzf key bindings and fuzzy completion (only available in 0.48.0 or later)
eval "$(fzf --zsh)"

Check that the key bindings were loaded:

bindkey -a | grep fzf

# output expected:
#
# "^R" fzf-history-widget  # CTRL + R: reverse history search
# "^T" fzf-file-widget     # CTRL + T: search files
# "^[c" fzf-cd-widget      # ALT  + C: search directories

Each widget reads its own environment variables, so you can tune it to your needs. This is how I configure them:

# fzf parameters used in all widgets - configure layout and wrapped the preview results (useful in large command rendering)
export FZF_DEFAULT_OPTS="--height 100% --layout reverse --preview-window=wrap"

# CTRL + R: put the selected history command in the preview window - "{}" will be replaced by item selected in fzf execution runtime
export FZF_CTRL_R_OPTS="--preview 'echo {}'"

# ALT + C: set "fd-find" as directory search engine instead of "find" and exclude "venv|virtualenv|.git" of the results during searching
export FZF_ALT_C_COMMAND="fd --type directory --exclude venv --exclude virtualenv --exclude .git"

# ALT + C: put the tree command output based on item selected
export FZF_ALT_C_OPTS="--preview 'tree -C {}'"

# CTRL + T: set "fd-find" as search engine instead of "find" and exclude "venv|virtualenv|.git" for the results
export FZF_CTRL_T_COMMAND="fd --exclude venv --exclude virtualenv --exclude .git"

# CTRL + T: put the file content if item select is a file, or put tree command output if item selected is directory
export FZF_CTRL_T_OPTS="--preview '[ -d {} ] && tree -C {} || bat --color=always --style=numbers {}'"

My full fzf configuration is in my ~/.zshrc: c-neto/ansible-configure-fedora

Results

  • fzf-history-widget, on Ctrl + R:

  • fzf-cd-widget, on Alt + C:

  • fzf-file-widget, on Ctrl + T:

  • Searching pods in a Kubernetes cluster with $ kgp -A | fzf:

Why I Recommend fzf

My search for a better command history search gave me much more than I expected. fzf taught me what a fuzzy finder is and what it’s for. It isn’t limited to history: you can pipe anything into it and search it interactively.

I think it’s a much better choice than the default history search in Zsh and Bash. Fish already has a good one, but fzf still adds file and directory search with previews. The search is very fast, and the environment variables let you shape every widget to the way you work. It had more than 59K stars on GitHub when I wrote this post, and I think it earns them. I approve and recommend it!

fzf widgets are regular Zsh widgets bound to keys. If you want to understand how that works, or write your own, I explain it in Hacking Your Zsh Terminal with Custom Widgets.

Key Takeaways

  • Ctrl + R, find, and command | grep all force you to know exactly what you’re looking for, or to repeat the search many times.

  • A fuzzy finder matches partial words, characters out of order, and typos, and filters the list as you type.

  • fzf reads any command’s output, so command | fzf replaces most command | grep searches.

  • eval "$(fzf --zsh)" (fzf 0.48.0 or later) loads three widgets: Ctrl + R for history, Ctrl + T for files, and Alt + C for directories.

  • Use fd as the search engine and bat and tree for previews, configured through the FZF_* environment variables.

References

  • fzf (GitHub)

  • fzf shell integrations (GitHub)

  • fd (GitHub)

  • bat (GitHub)

  • tree command (nixCraft)

  • Zsh (zsh.org)

  • My fzf configuration in ~/.zshrc (GitHub)

  • Extra: skim, a fuzzy finder written in Rust (GitHub)

entry.title: ZSH + Starship: A Productivity Masterpiece
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2024/02/08

This blog post covers how I ended up with ZSH and Starship as my terminal setup. It walks through the shells I tried along the way, my favorite ZSH plugins and ZSH options, my minimal Starship configuration, and a step-by-step guide to reproduce it from scratch.

The Shells I Tried

Productivity is a topic I really enjoy. For a long time, I used a plain Bash terminal. It forced me to memorize commands, but it did not make me productive, so I decided to improve my setup.

xonsh: Python + Bash Advantages (and Disadvantages)

Because I work a lot with Python, I used xonsh for about six months. xonsh is a superset of Python with extra shell primitives that Bash users already know. Mixing Python syntax with Bash commands is productive, but debugging can get hard. Imagine a Python list comprehension combined with dictionaries and Bash environment variables in the same line.

zsh: Extensible and Production-Ready (If Customized)

I wanted to come back to a more conventional shell, so I gave ZSH a chance. ZSH is a highly customizable shell with a large plugin ecosystem. It won me over, especially with Spaceship, a “minimalistic, powerful and extremely customizable ZSH prompt”, and oh-my-zsh, a framework that manages plugins and themes. I thought I had found a stable balance between productivity and simplicity, but on my macOS workstation, the input and startup delay got on my nerves.

I searched blog posts and YouTube videos for tips, but nothing fixed it. So I installed the plugins manually, without oh-my-zsh, and tried Starship. In my words, Starship is “a Spaceship alternative, written in Rust, blazing fast, with many stars on GitHub”.

The results were great. Moving my theme from Spaceship to Starship took almost no effort, and the performance was exactly what I wanted.

fish: Ready to Use (But Not POSIX-Compliant)

More recently, I tried Fish, described as “a smart and user-friendly command line shell”. Its performance and default features impressed me, and Starship supports it too. Out of the box, Fish already has syntax checking with color indicators, autosuggestions based on history, and a selection menu for command options and arguments. It’s simple and ready to use.

The drawback is that Fish does not follow the POSIX sh definition. For example, $ FOOBAR=123 does not declare a variable. You have to write $ set FOOBAR 123 instead. That rules Fish out of my daily work, but if ZSH were not an option, I would happily use it.

My Favorite ZSH Plugins

ZSH has a huge number of plugins. They are usually installed and managed by oh-my-zsh, but you can install them directly, because a plugin is just a script file with a set of functions. These are the ones I can’t work without.

zsh-autosuggestions: Remembers Commands for You

This is my favorite plugin, no doubt. It copies a Fish feature: as you type, it suggests a completion based on your history.

More Details: zsh-users/zsh-autosuggestions

zsh-syntax-highlighting: Valid Commands by Color

Another plugin inspired by Fish. When a command is typed correctly, it turns green. Otherwise, it turns red, so you catch typos before pressing Enter.

More Details: zsh-users/zsh-syntax-highlighting

kubectl: The k Alias for kubectl

This plugin adds Kubernetes completion and short aliases for common kubectl commands. For example:

# shortcut for: kubectl get pods
$ kgp

# shortcut for: kubectl delete cm foobar-config-map
$ kdelcm foobar-config-map

# shortcut for: kubectl get cronjob
$ k get cj

More Details: ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh/plugins/kubectl

I use the same kind of aliases when I study for the Kubernetes certifications. My workstation setup for the CKA, CKAD, and CKS exams covers the ones that save the most time.

My Starship Configuration

Simplicity is elegance. My Starship prompt shows only the information I care about:

  • aws: only the profile name of my AWS session.

  • git: only the branch, nothing else.

  • python: the active virtualenv.

  • kubernetes: the Kubernetes context name. I style it differently depending on the name, so study, test, and production clusters are easy to tell apart.

My full ~/.config/starship.toml: c-neto/ansible-configure-fedora/files/dotfiles/starship.toml

My Favorite ZSH Options (setopt)

Some features that Bash or Fish have by default, such as comments in the prompt or sharing history, must be enabled explicitly in ZSH. You enable them with setopt in ~/.zshrc. Running $ set -o lists every option and whether it’s on, and the ZSH Options Reference describes each one.

These are the options I enable:

  • INTERACTIVE_COMMENTS: allows # comments in the interactive shell.

  • APPEND_HISTORY: appends new entries to the history file instead of overwriting it.

  • INC_APPEND_HISTORY: writes each command to the history file as soon as it runs.

  • HIST_IGNORE_DUPS: does not record a command that repeats the previous one, which also makes zsh-autosuggestions faster.

  • HIST_IGNORE_SPACE: does not record commands that start with a space.

My full ~/.zshrc: c-neto/ansible-configure-fedora/files/dotfiles/.zshrc

How to Set Up My ZSH + Starship From Scratch

All my dotfiles are on GitHub: c-neto/ansible-configure-fedora/files/dotfiles/

  • 1 optional: Back up your current dotfiles (~/.zshrc and ~/.zsh_history):

$ cp "$HOME/.zshrc" "$HOME/.zshrc.backup"
$ cp "$HOME/.zsh_history" "$HOME/.zsh_history.backup"

  • 2: Install ZSH with your package manager.

# if Linux (Fedora)
$ dnf install zsh

# if MacOS
$ brew install zsh

  • 3: Install Starship:

$ curl -sS https://starship.rs/install.sh | sh

About Nerd Fonts:

The ~/.config/starship.toml file from step 5 does not need Nerd Fonts. If emojis don’t render correctly, installing one may help.

  • 4: Create the directories for the ZSH plugins and the Starship configuration:

$ mkdir "$HOME/.config/"
$ mkdir "$HOME/.my-custom-zsh/"

  • 5: Download my ~/.config/starship.toml:

$ curl 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/c-neto/ansible-configure-fedora/main/files/dotfiles/starship.toml' > "$HOME/.config/starship.toml"

  • 6: Install the plugins manually:

# k alias
$ curl 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh/master/plugins/kubectl/kubectl.plugin.zsh' > "$HOME/.my-custom-zsh/kubectl.plugin.zsh"

# zsh-syntax-highlighting
$ git clone --depth 1 'https://github.com/zsh-users/zsh-syntax-highlighting.git' "$HOME/.my-custom-zsh/zsh-syntax-highlighting"

# zsh-autosuggestions
$ git clone --depth 1 'https://github.com/zsh-users/zsh-autosuggestions' "$HOME/.my-custom-zsh/zsh-autosuggestions"

  • 7: Download my ~/.zshrc:

$ curl 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/c-neto/ansible-configure-fedora/main/files/dotfiles/.zshrc' > "$HOME/.zshrc"

Key Binding Tip

You can change the bindkey values to your preference. To find the code for a key, run $ cat -v and press the key: its code appears in the shell. Then map functions such as forward-word and backward-word to that code.

More details about the bindkey standard widgets: https://zsh.sourceforge.io/Doc/Release/Zsh-Line-Editor.html#Zle-Widgets

  • 8: Restart your terminal. The result looks like this:

Why I Settled on ZSH + Starship

Productivity is a moving target. Tools should fit what you need now, and it’s fine to change them when your work changes.

For my DevOps routine today, ZSH with Starship is a balanced, cross-platform choice with good performance, productivity, and room to extend. If you want to go further, ZSH also lets you write your own key bindings, which I cover in Hacking Your Zsh Terminal with Custom Widgets, and fzf turns history and file search into an interactive menu.

Fish still gets an honorable mention: its default configuration inspired most of the plugins I use in ZSH.

Key Takeaways

  • xonsh mixes Python and Bash productively, but debugging mixed syntax gets hard.

  • oh-my-zsh is convenient, but on my macOS machine it made startup and input noticeably slow. Installing plugins manually fixed that.

  • Starship is a fast, Rust-based prompt that replaced Spaceship with almost no configuration changes.

  • Fish is excellent out of the box, but it is not POSIX-compliant, which rules it out for my daily work.

  • zsh-autosuggestions, zsh-syntax-highlighting, and the kubectl plugin bring Fish-like features and Kubernetes aliases to ZSH.

  • Enable INTERACTIVE_COMMENTS and the history options with setopt in ~/.zshrc.

  • Keep the prompt minimal: show only the context you check all the time, such as git branch, AWS profile, virtualenv, and Kubernetes context.

References

  • ZSH (zsh.org)

  • Options (ZSH manual)

  • Zle widgets (ZSH manual)

  • Starship (starship.rs)

  • Starship source (GitHub)

  • zsh-autosuggestions (GitHub)

  • zsh-syntax-highlighting (GitHub)

  • kubectl plugin (oh-my-zsh)

  • xonsh (xon.sh)

  • oh-my-zsh (ohmyz.sh)

  • Spaceship prompt (GitHub)

  • Shell Command Language (POSIX)

  • My dotfiles: .zshrc and starship.toml

entry.title: Systemd Drop-in Overrides: Customize Unit Properties Without Editing the Unit File
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2023/11/19

This blog post covers a cleaner way to customize a systemd service. Instead of editing the unit file, you put your changes in an override.conf drop-in file that systemd merges on top of the original. It explains why direct edits cause problems, how overrides work, and walks through a hands-on example.

Why Editing the Unit File Directly Causes Problems

Sometimes you need to change a property of a systemd service, such as an environment variable that raises the debug level while you troubleshoot. The traditional way is to edit the unit file directly. For example, to change a Docker property, you edit /etc/systemd/system/docker.service, reload systemd with $ systemctl daemon-reload, and restart the service with $ systemctl restart docker.

That works, but it causes a few problems:

  • Editing the default unit file makes it easier to break the service with a wrong setting.

  • Custom changes are hard to spot later if nobody commented them.

  • A package update can replace the unit file and silently drop your changes. Package managers such as rpm or apt own those files.

How Systemd Overrides Work

A drop-in file is a .conf file in a <unit>.d/ directory that systemd reads after the unit file and merges on top of it. As the systemd.unit documentation describes, this lets you change unit properties while the original file stays untouched.

The convention for overrides is this path:

/etc/systemd/system/<UNIT-SERVICE-NAME>.service.d/override.conf

<UNIT-SERVICE-NAME> is a placeholder.

Properties in override.conf take precedence over the ones in <UNIT-SERVICE-NAME>.service. There is one catch: settings that accept a list, such as ExecStart=, add to the original value instead of replacing it. To replace them, first assign an empty value to reset the list, then set the new one. The example below shows the default unit and the override side by side:

  • Default Properties

/etc/systemd/system/my-script.service
[Unit]
Description=My script
; collapsed parameters...

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/my-script.sh --prod

[Install]
; collapsed parameters...

  • Override Properties

/etc/systemd/system/my-script.service.d/override.conf
[Service]
ExecStart=
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/my-script.sh --dev

When my-script.service starts, it runs my-script.sh --dev. The empty ExecStart= in override.conf clears the command from the unit file, and the next line sets the new one.

The systemctl edit command is the shortcut for all of this. $ systemctl edit <UNIT-SERVICE-NAME> creates /etc/systemd/system/<UNIT-SERVICE-NAME>.service.d/override.conf, opens your editor, and runs $ systemctl daemon-reload for you when you close it. The only step left is $ systemctl restart <UNIT-SERVICE-NAME> when the change needs a restart.

Hands-On: Overriding an EnvironmentFile

This example creates a service called my-script and then overrides where it reads its environment variables from. It uses these files:

/tmp/my-script/env_custom.env           # env vars source of the my-script process
/tmp/my-script/env_default.env          # other env vars source of the my-script process
/tmp/my-script/my-script.sh             # script that my-script process run
/etc/systemd/system/my-script.service   # unit service file definition

The files are on my GitHub: c-neto/my-devops-labs/blog/2023-11-19

First, create the working directory for the script:

$ mkdir /tmp/my-script/

Then create the script itself. It prints two environment variables every second:

$ vim /tmp/my-script/my-script.sh
#!/bin/bash

while true; do
  echo ">>> $APP_NAME - $MY_CUSTOM_ENV_VAR"
  sleep 1
done

Make it executable:

$ chmod +x /tmp/my-script/my-script.sh

Next, create the two files that will provide environment variables to the service:

$ vim /tmp/my-script/env_default.env
APP_NAME="My Awesome Script"
MY_CUSTOM_ENV_VAR="Irish Blood"
$ vim /tmp/my-script/env_custom.env
MY_CUSTOM_ENV_VAR="English Heart"

Now create the unit file. ExecStart= uses the absolute path of the script, because systemd does not search WorkingDirectory for the executable.

$ vim /etc/systemd/system/my-script.service
[Service]
WorkingDirectory=/tmp/my-script/
ExecStart=/tmp/my-script/my-script.sh
EnvironmentFile=/tmp/my-script/env_default.env

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Reload systemd so it picks up the new unit, then start the service:

$ systemctl daemon-reload
$ systemctl start my-script

The log shows the values from env_default.env:

$ journalctl -u my-script -f
Nov 19 16:11:29 fedora my-script.sh[33631]: >>> My Awesome Script - Irish Blood
Nov 19 16:11:30 fedora my-script.sh[33631]: >>> My Awesome Script - Irish Blood

Now override the environment file. Create the drop-in directory:

$ mkdir /etc/systemd/system/my-script.service.d/

Then add a second EnvironmentFile in override.conf:

$ vim /etc/systemd/system/my-script.service.d/override.conf
[Service]
EnvironmentFile=/tmp/my-script/env_custom.env

After $ systemctl daemon-reload and $ systemctl restart my-script, the log changes:

$ journalctl -u my-script -f
Nov 19 16:21:42 fedora my-script.sh[58573]: >>> My Awesome Script - English Heart
Nov 19 16:21:43 fedora my-script.sh[58573]: >>> My Awesome Script - English Heart

EnvironmentFile= is a list setting, so the override adds env_custom.env after env_default.env instead of replacing it. Both files are read, and when the same variable appears in both, the later file wins. That is why APP_NAME still comes from env_default.env, while MY_CUSTOM_ENV_VAR now comes from env_custom.env.

Why I Prefer Overrides

Overrides keep the original unit file intact and put every custom setting in one explicit place. When something breaks, $ systemctl cat <UNIT-SERVICE-NAME> shows the unit file and every drop-in, so you can see right away what was changed. They also survive package updates, because the package manager (dnf, apt, brew) only owns the original unit file, not your drop-in.

$ systemctl edit makes the whole process quick: one command to create the file, edit it, and reload systemd. For me, it is the default way to change any service I did not write myself. The kubelet is a good example: its log rotation flags can be set as a systemd Environment= property, as I show in Kubernetes Logs Simplified, and an override keeps that change out of the packaged unit file.

Key Takeaways

  • Editing a unit file directly makes mistakes harder to spot, and a package update can overwrite your changes.

  • A drop-in file at /etc/systemd/system/<unit>.service.d/override.conf is merged on top of the unit file, which stays untouched.

  • $ systemctl edit <unit> creates the drop-in, opens your editor, and reloads systemd.

  • List settings such as ExecStart= and EnvironmentFile= are added to, not replaced. Assign an empty value first to reset them.

  • With several EnvironmentFile= entries, a variable from a later file overrides the same variable from an earlier one.

  • $ systemctl cat <unit> shows the unit file and all its drop-ins together.

References

  • systemd.unit: drop-in files (systemd)

  • systemd.exec: EnvironmentFile= (systemd)

  • systemctl: edit and cat commands (systemd)

  • systemd project (systemd.io)

  • systemd cheat sheet (Red Hat)

  • Lab files for this post (GitHub)

I’m Carlos Neto, and this blog is where I share my experiences and open source contributions. More about me on my home page. If you have questions or a different approach, contact me on LinkedIn.

entry.title: Logstash Modular Pipelines: Reusing Inputs, Filters, and Outputs Without Duplication
entry.content:
Blog Post Publish Date: 2023/11/12

This blog post covers a Logstash pipeline structure that removes duplicated code. Each input, filter, and output lives in its own file, and every application’s pipeline is composed from those modules with a glob pattern and an environment variable. It includes an example configuration, a Docker Compose lab to try it, and my opinion on when the structure is worth it.

How a Logstash Pipeline Is Structured

Logstash is a great tool for building log pipelines. Its plugins cover ingestion, processing, enrichment, and delivery to other systems. A Logstash pipeline is a configuration written in the Logstash configuration DSL (Domain-Specific Language), a high-level language designed for log processing.

According to the configuration file structure documentation, a pipeline has three main sections:

  • input: where the logs come from.

  • filter: how they are parsed, processed, and enriched.

  • output: where the processed logs are sent.

The Problem: More Pipelines, More Duplicated Code

As the number of pipelines grows, so does the duplicated code. For simple needs, one file with input, filter, and output together is enough. With large applications, such as distributed services on Kubernetes, avoiding duplication becomes one of the main challenges.

When several applications need different processing logic, there are two common approaches, and both have a cost:

  • One shared pipeline with conditionals. The filter section checks a field such as a tag to decide which logic to apply. This avoids duplicating input and output, but it adds overhead to the filter section and makes it harder to find which application has a problem in the Logstash API metrics.

  • One pipeline per application. Each application gets its own configuration file. This removes the filter overhead, but every pipeline repeats the same input and output configuration.

The Solution: Modular Pipelines

The structure I use takes the good part of both approaches: split the pipeline sections (input, filter, output) into separate files, and load only the ones each application needs into its own dedicated pipeline.

Two Logstash features make this possible. Glob pattern support lets path.config load several files at once, and environment variables let you choose those files outside the configuration.

Configuration Example

The first step is to create the modules: each input, filter, and output goes in its own file, focused on one job.

$ tree /usr/share/logstash/pipeline/
├── filter-app-a.cfg        # filter of the application-a logic parser
├── filter-app-b.cfg        # filter of the application-b logic parser
├── input-http.cfg          # input to receive logs from http protocol
├── input-rabbitmq.cfg      # input to receive logs from rabbitmq queue
├── output-opensearch.cfg   # output to forward logs processed to opensearch server 
└── output-http.cfg         # output to forward logs processed to http server

Next, define one pipeline per application, with path.config pointing to an environment variable:

$ cat /usr/share/logstash/config/pipeline.yml
- pipeline.id: application-a-pipeline
  path.config: "/usr/share/logstash/pipeline/${LOGSTASH_PIPELINE_APPLICATION_A}.cfg"

- pipeline.id: application-b-pipeline
  path.config: "/usr/share/logstash/pipeline/${LOGSTASH_PIPELINE_APPLICATION_B}.cfg"

Finally, set each variable to a glob pattern that lists the modules for that pipeline:

$ env
LOGSTASH_PIPELINE_APPLICATION_A="{input-http,input-rabbitmq,filter-app-a,output-opensearch,output-http}"
LOGSTASH_PIPELINE_APPLICATION_B="{input-http,filter-app-b,output-opensearch}"

With these values, application-a-pipeline receives logs from HTTP and RabbitMQ, parses them with filter-app-a.cfg, and sends them to both OpenSearch and an HTTP server. application-b-pipeline receives logs only from HTTP, parses them with filter-app-b.cfg, and sends them only to OpenSearch.

Advantages of the Modular Structure

  • No duplicated code. The same module can be used by many pipelines, for example one input and one output shared by all of them.

  • Flexible composition. A pipeline can load several modules of the same type, such as two outputs and three inputs.

  • Simpler filters. Each filter file holds only one application’s parsing logic, with no conditionals on tags to decide which logic to run.

  • Easier troubleshooting. Each application keeps its own pipeline, so the Logstash metrics API still shows which one is slow or failing.

  • Easier tests. Because inputs and outputs are chosen by an environment variable, you can test a filter with a mock input and stdout as the output, and check that the logic works before deploying it.

I created a Docker Compose lab to try this structure. You can find it on my GitHub: c-neto/my-devops-labs/blog/2023-11-12.

When the Modular Structure Is Worth It

Logstash handles both small and large workloads, and this structure is one way, not the only way, to deal with pipelines that keep growing. With only a few applications, it can add complexity you don’t need.

I have used this structure and seen a big improvement in maintainability, especially in testing: I can test my filter logic by changing a single environment variable. My main goal is always to make pipelines easier to maintain, but every context has its own challenges. I recommend this structure when pipeline maintenance is getting hard, duplicated code is growing, and the Logstash configuration has become error-prone.

If you are sending these logs to OpenSearch, two related posts may help: Logstash Sniffing for spreading ingestion across a scalable cluster, and Logstash DB Enrichment for adding database data to events inside a filter.

Key Takeaways

  • A Logstash pipeline has three sections: input, filter, and output.

  • One shared pipeline with conditionals overloads the filter section. One file per application duplicates input and output.

  • Split each section into its own file, and compose each application’s pipeline from those modules.

  • path.config with an environment variable and a glob pattern such as {input-http,filter-app-a,output-opensearch} selects the modules per pipeline.

  • Separate pipelines keep the Logstash metrics API useful for troubleshooting each application.

  • Swapping inputs and outputs through an environment variable makes it easy to test filter logic with mock data and stdout.

  • With only a few applications, a single simple pipeline may be enough.

References

  • Structure of a pipeline (Logstash)

  • Glob pattern support (Logstash)

  • Using environment variables (Logstash)

  • Docker Compose lab for this post (GitHub)

I’m Carlos Neto, and I’ve been running OpenSearch on EKS for over five years. More about me on my home page. If you have questions or a different approach, contact me on LinkedIn.
